query:
Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: a charge is induction-melted in a crucible,
argon over-pressure ("graining" pressure) pushes the melt through a bottom nozzle once a stopper
(sealing) rod is lifted, the stream falls onto an inclined plate driven by an ultrasonic sonotrode
(booster plus horn), and melt that the plate does not atomize runs off into a catch crucible below.
A separate "turbo" button applies 1.5 bar to push the melt out (it replaces, rather than adds to, the
graining pressure). Pressures are read on the HMI; whether they are gauge or absolute is unconfirmed.

Alloy: nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 ("630 bronze" rod; Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%; liquidus ~1054 C;
liquid density ~6.9-7.0 g/cm3; surface tension ~1.1-1.3 N/m). Melt setpoint 1300 C (the module's
hard limit; ~245 C superheat), read by a thermocouple at the crucible. Crucible: graphite (material to
be confirmed) with its interior sprayed with a boron nitride paint; BN stopper rod; hBN nozzle (bore
about 0.5 mm, to be confirmed). Plate: carbon-fiber composite coated with tungsten (the vendor's
W-coated plate for copper alloys). Booster 1:1.5. Argon atmosphere. In training with aluminum, the
vendor's trainer set the plate so that the melt landed on the plate and rolled down about a third of
the plate's length before it atomized.

Run A (27 Oct): new plate, fresh BN coat, new nozzle, 1080 g charge (four rod pieces), O2 24 ppm,
amplitude 90%, graining 0.19 bar, held 2 min after the charge melted. The stream hit right at the
lower (free) end of the plate. The melt kept flowing only while the operator held the turbo (1.5 bar)
for most of the run; ~97% of the charge was collected as powder, with a visible fraction of flakes.
A thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling, BN came away with
it: light grey crescents of BN on the underside of the skull match the bare patches in the crucible's
coat.

Run B (28 Oct): the same plate (second use; it looked fine), the same nozzle (the bore looked clear),
the same crucible with small bare patches where the BN had come off (not recoated), 858 g charge (five
rod pieces), O2 11 ppm, amplitude 90% for the first quarter of the pour, then 100%; graining 0.23 bar
at the start, back to 0.19 bar about halfway; held 1 min after melting. The plate was moved up a little
so that the stream landed farther up the plate rather than at its very end. Result: the melt "really
struggled to atomize"; some powder was made, but most of the charge ended up as a solid puck in the
catch crucible. Changing amplitude and pressure during the pour did not help.

Focus on the ultrasonic atomization itself and what differed between run A and run B. Give numbers
with sources (DOIs) and show the inputs to any estimate.

1. Capillary-wave atomization needs a thin melt film that wets the plate and a vibration amplitude
   above threshold. For liquid C63000 at 1150-1300 C (viscosity ~4-5 mPa s) and, for comparison,
   liquid aluminum, estimate the capillary wavelength and median droplet size at 20, 35 and 40 kHz,
   the threshold amplitude, the thickest film that still atomizes, and the largest mass flow rate a
   plate can atomize per unit area and per unit acoustic power. How does NAB's ~2.8x higher density
   than aluminum change the needed amplitude, the plate's capacity, and how far the film runs down an
   inclined plate before it atomizes?
2. Plate position: for a plate driven by a sonotrode, how does the vibration amplitude vary over the
   plate (flexural modes, nodal lines, the free end versus near the horn)? If the stream lands higher
   up the plate instead of at its free end, could it fall near a node or a low-amplitude zone and fail
   to atomize? How should the impact point be chosen and checked (for example a powder or water
   pattern on the vibrating plate, or a laser vibrometer)?
3. Plate reuse: what does one ~1 kg run of NAB do to a W-coated carbon-fiber plate (adhered metal or
   an Al2O3 film, coating dissolution or cracking where the stream landed, poorer wetting of an
   oxidized surface, added mass that detunes the resonance, a joint to the sonotrode loosened by
   thermal cycling)? Estimate the frequency shift from a few grams of adhered metal. Which of these
   could make a second run fail? How should the plate be inspected and cleaned between runs, and which
   generator readings (frequency, power, amplitude, overload or error flags) show a detuned or
   damaged plate?
4. Flow rate versus capacity: estimate the mass flow through a 0.5 mm and a 1 mm nozzle at 0.19 and
   0.23 bar and at 1.5 bar turbo, with the metallostatic head of 858 g versus 1080 g in a crucible of
   ~50-60 mm inner diameter, and say whether exceeding the plate's capacity makes melt run off the plate
   into the catch crucible. Does run A's success with turbo held suggest the plate can take high flow
   when the stream lands at the free end?
5. Thermal effects: plate temperature during the pour, cooling of the film on the plate, freezing or
   solid build-up on the plate that stops atomization, the effect of a 1 min versus 2 min hold on the
   melt temperature reaching the nozzle, and whether raising amplitude from 90% to 100% mid-pour helps
   or hurts (transducer heating, frequency drift, splashing).
6. Rank the candidate causes of run B's failure by likelihood, and give a plan for the next run: which
   single variable to change first, what to log (generator frequency and power, pressures, where the
   stream lands, video), a plate-position rule for NAB versus aluminum, and pass/fail criteria.
task_summary: Analyze Ultrasonic Capillary Wave Atomization Differences Between Two NAB Runs And Provide Quantitative Estimates

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only

        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double

        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider
        - INVESTIGATOR: Investigator
        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: a charge is induction-melted in a crucible,
argon over-pressure ("graining" pressure) pushes the melt through a bottom nozzle once a stopper
(sealing) rod is lifted, the stream falls onto an inclined plate driven by an ultrasonic sonotrode
(booster plus horn), and melt that the plate does not atomize runs off into a catch crucible below.
A separate "turbo" button applies 1.5 bar to push the melt out (it replaces, rather than adds to, the
graining pressure). Pressures are read on the HMI; whether they are gauge or absolute is unconfirmed.

Alloy: nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 ("630 bronze" rod; Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%; liquidus ~1054 C;
liquid density ~6.9-7.0 g/cm3; surface tension ~1.1-1.3 N/m). Melt setpoint 1300 C (the module's
hard limit; ~245 C superheat), read by a thermocouple at the crucible. Crucible: graphite (material to
be confirmed) with its interior sprayed with a boron nitride paint; BN stopper rod; hBN nozzle (bore
about 0.5 mm, to be confirmed). Plate: carbon-fiber composite coated with tungsten (the vendor's
W-coated plate for copper alloys). Booster 1:1.5. Argon atmosphere. In training with aluminum, the
vendor's trainer set the plate so that the melt landed on the plate and rolled down about a third of
the plate's length before it atomized.

Run A (27 Oct): new plate, fresh BN coat, new nozzle, 1080 g charge (four rod pieces), O2 24 ppm,
amplitude 90%, graining 0.19 bar, held 2 min after the charge melted. The stream hit right at the
lower (free) end of the plate. The melt kept flowing only while the operator held the turbo (1.5 bar)
for most of the run; ~97% of the charge was collected as powder, with a visible fraction of flakes.
A thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling, BN came away with
it: light grey crescents of BN on the underside of the skull match the bare patches in the crucible's
coat.

Run B (28 Oct): the same plate (second use; it looked fine), the same nozzle (the bore looked clear),
the same crucible with small bare patches where the BN had come off (not recoated), 858 g charge (five
rod pieces), O2 11 ppm, amplitude 90% for the first quarter of the pour, then 100%; graining 0.23 bar
at the start, back to 0.19 bar about halfway; held 1 min after melting. The plate was moved up a little
so that the stream landed farther up the plate rather than at its very end. Result: the melt "really
struggled to atomize"; some powder was made, but most of the charge ended up as a solid puck in the
catch crucible. Changing amplitude and pressure during the pour did not help.

Focus on the ultrasonic atomization itself and what differed between run A and run B. Give numbers
with sources (DOIs) and show the inputs to any estimate.

1. Capillary-wave atomization needs a thin melt film that wets the plate and a vibration amplitude
   above threshold. For liquid C63000 at 1150-1300 C (viscosity ~4-5 mPa s) and, for comparison,
   liquid aluminum, estimate the capillary wavelength and median droplet size at 20, 35 and 40 kHz,
   the threshold amplitude, the thickest film that still atomizes, and the largest mass flow rate a
   plate can atomize per unit area and per unit acoustic power. How does NAB's ~2.8x higher density
   than aluminum change the needed amplitude, the plate's capacity, and how far the film runs down an
   inclined plate before it atomizes?
2. Plate position: for a plate driven by a sonotrode, how does the vibration amplitude vary over the
   plate (flexural modes, nodal lines, the free end versus near the horn)? If the stream lands higher
   up the plate instead of at its free end, could it fall near a node or a low-amplitude zone and fail
   to atomize? How should the impact point be chosen and checked (for example a powder or water
   pattern on the vibrating plate, or a laser vibrometer)?
3. Plate reuse: what does one ~1 kg run of NAB do to a W-coated carbon-fiber plate (adhered metal or
   an Al2O3 film, coating dissolution or cracking where the stream landed, poorer wetting of an
   oxidized surface, added mass that detunes the resonance, a joint to the sonotrode loosened by
   thermal cycling)? Estimate the frequency shift from a few grams of adhered metal. Which of these
   could make a second run fail? How should the plate be inspected and cleaned between runs, and which
   generator readings (frequency, power, amplitude, overload or error flags) show a detuned or
   damaged plate?
4. Flow rate versus capacity: estimate the mass flow through a 0.5 mm and a 1 mm nozzle at 0.19 and
   0.23 bar and at 1.5 bar turbo, with the metallostatic head of 858 g versus 1080 g in a crucible of
   ~50-60 mm inner diameter, and say whether exceeding the plate's capacity makes melt run off the plate
   into the catch crucible. Does run A's success with turbo held suggest the plate can take high flow
   when the stream lands at the free end?
5. Thermal effects: plate temperature during the pour, cooling of the film on the plate, freezing or
   solid build-up on the plate that stops atomization, the effect of a 1 min versus 2 min hold on the
   melt temperature reaching the nozzle, and whether raising amplitude from 90% to 100% mid-pour helps
   or hurts (transducer heating, frequency drift, splashing).
6. Rank the candidate causes of run B's failure by likelihood, and give a plan for the next run: which
   single variable to change first, what to log (generator frequency and power, pressures, where the
   stream lands, video), a plate-position rule for NAB versus aluminum, and pass/fail criteria.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Spray drying derived for the synthesis of nano or submicron-sized powders with distinct functionalization and structure. Even after decades of development, producing fine droplets with a uniform size distribution and high production rate in an atomizer is still a challenge. The purpose of this study is to review the significance of the latest advances in ultrasonic atomization and how they have affected spray drying technology, which is essential to the improvement of powder synthesis and processing. Furthermore, ultrasonic atomization can be used to evaluate the usefulness of developed in powder engineering for a variety of applications. These observations offer important insights into the behavior of the droplets generated by the ultrasonic atomizer inside the particular spray dryer reactors that are being used. Numerous researchers have reported their innovations in spray dryer equipped with either Ultrasonic Vibrating Mesh Atomizers (UVM-As) and Surface Acoustic Wave Atomizer (SAW-As) which is known as Ultrasonic Atomizer. Understanding the fundamentals of ultrasonic atomization enables the advancement of spray dryer innovations and technology. Therefore, recent advances in spray drying technology indicate that more compact system designs can be achieved without compromising energy efficiency, thereby contributing to improved overall process performance. In this context, systematic evaluation of atomizer performance is essential at the early stages of atomizer development, particularly in terms of droplet size distribution, energy consumption, and operational stability. Based on the collective findings reported in the literature, vibrating mesh atomizer-assisted spray drying has demonstrated significant potential for producing finer particles with narrower size distributions, making it a promising atomization approach for advanced spray drying applications.

Abstract:
A two-phase flow axisymmetric numerical model was proposed to understand liquid metal droplet formation in a co-flowing capillary microfluidics device based on a phase field model. The droplet detachment processes were observed in the experiment and are in good agreement with the simulation method. The effects of the viscosities and flowrates of the continuous phase fluid, interfacial tension as well as the wetting property of the metallic needle against the bulk liquid metal on the droplet formation and production rate were numerically investigated. It was found that the droplet diameter decreased with the increment of the viscosities and flowrates of the outer phase carrier fluid. The dispersed phase fluid with high interfacial tension tended to prolong the time for equilibrium between the viscous drag force and interfacial tension on the liquid–liquid fluid surface, delaying the droplet to be pinched off from the capillary orifice and causing large droplet diameter. Finally, the wetting performance of the metallic needle against the liquid metal was explored. The result indicate that the droplet diameter became less dependent on the contact angle while the size distribution of the liquid metal droplet was affected by their wetting performance. A more hydrophilic wetting performance were expected to prepare liquid metal droplet with more monodispersity. The numerical model and simulation results provide the feasibility of predicting the droplet formation with a high surface tension in a glass capillary microfluidic device.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Gas atomization is a key technology for producing high-quality metal powders, widely adopted in additive manufacturing and other powder-based industries due to its versatility and productivity. Its complexity, such as intense gas&ndash;liquid momentum exchange, thermal gradients in solidification, and multiple influencing factors, poses significant challenges for process control. This comprehensive review explores the complexities of gas atomization technology in metal powder production, examining the underlying mechanisms, simulation techniques, flow field dynamics, and key influencing factors. It clarifies that primary atomization is characterized by liquid film atomization, driven by Kelvin&ndash;Helmholtz instabilities, and fountain atomization, triggered by Rayleigh&ndash;Taylor instabilities. Secondary atomization, on the other hand, is predominantly influenced by shear and inertial forces. The review emphasizes the key roles of physical gas and liquid properties, temperature, pressure, nozzle design, and solidification processes in determining the characteristics of the resulting metal powder. It concludes that a thorough understanding of these factors is essential for refining the atomization process and improving the quality of the metal powder produced. The review suggests that future research should focus on resolving discrepancies in atomization mechanisms, enhancing simulation methodologies, and investigating the effects of advanced nozzle designs on the production of metal powder.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The novel drug delivery system refers to the formulations and technologies for transporting a pharmaceutical compound in the body as it is needed to safely achieve its desired therapeutic effects. In this study, the onset vibrational amplitude of capillary surface waves for ultrasonic atomization spray is explained based on Faraday instability. Using ultrasonic frequency, the vibrational amplitude approached a critical point, and the liquid surface broke up into tiny drops. The micro-droplets were are steadily and continuously formed after the liquid feeding rate was optimized. The simulation study reported a minimum vibrational amplitude or onset value of 0.38 μm at 500 kHz frequency. The required minimum energy to atomize the drops was simulated by COMSOL Multiphysics simulation software. The simulation result agreed well with the numerical results of a subharmonic vibrational model that ocurred at 250 kHz frequency on the liquid surface. This newly designed single frequency ultrasonic atomizer showed its true physical characteristic of resonance on the fluid surface plane. Hence, this research will contribute to the future development of a single-frequency ultrasonic nebulizer and mechatronics for the generation of uniform atomized droplets.</jats:p>

    author = "Kooij, Stefan and Astefanei, Alina and Corthals, Garry L. and Bonn, Daniel",

    year = "2019",

Abstract:
In many applications where small, similar-sized droplets are needed, ultrasonic nebulizers are employed. Little is known about the mechanism of nebulization, for example about what determines the median droplet size. Even less understood, is the droplet size distribution, which is often simply fitted with a log-normal distribution or assumed to be very narrow. We perform the first systematic study of droplet size distributions for different nebulizer technologies, showing that these distributions can be very well fitted with distributions found for sprays, where the size distribution is completely determined by the corrugation of ligaments and the distribution of ligament sizes. In our case, breakup is believed to be due to pinch-off of Faraday instabilities. The droplet size distribution is then set by the distribution of wavelengths of the standing capillary waves and the roughness of the pinch-off ligaments. We show that different nebulizer technologies produce different size distributions, which we relate to (variation in) wavelengths of the waves that contribute to the droplet formation. We further show that the median droplet size scales with the capillary wavelength, with a proportionality constant that depends only slightly on the type of nebulizer, despite order-of-magnitude differences in other parameters.

Abstract:
Ultrasonic atomization of liquids into micrometer-diameter droplets is crucial across multiple fields, ranging from drug delivery, to spectrometry and printing. Controlling the size and uniformity of the generated droplets on-demand is crucial in all these applications. However, existing systems lack the required precision to tune the droplet properties, and the underlying droplet formation mechanism under high-frequency ultrasonic actuation remains poorly understood due to experimental constraints. Here, we present an atomization platform, which overcomes these current limitations. Our device utilizes oscillating high aspect ratio micro-channels to extract liquids from various inlets (ranging from sessile droplets to large beakers), bound them in a precisely defined narrow region, and, controllably atomize them on-demand. The droplet size can be precisely dialled from 3.6 μm to 6.8 μm by simply tuning the actuation parameters. Since the approach does not need nozzles, meshes or impacting jets, stresses exerted on the liquid samples are reduced, hence it is gentler on delicate samples. The precision offered by the technique allows us for the first time to experimentally visualise the oscillating fluid interface at the onset of atomization at MHz frequencies, and demonstrate its applications for targeted respiratory drug delivery.

Abstract:
Ultrasonic atomization is an object of steadily increasing interest from metal powder manufacturers, both for additive manufacturing and powder metallurgy. Based on the analysis of available theoretical studies, simulations and experiments, it was noted that the average particle size after atomization and the final particle size distribution depend on the process parameters (e.g., frequency, amplitude) and the parameters of the atomized fluid (e.g., viscosity, surface tension). The objective of this study is to evaluate the feasibility of using ultrasonic atomization to study the properties of liquid metals. It attempts to close a gap in existing knowledge in searching for a new, possibly simple and cost-effective method to study the properties of liquid metals and clarify the relationship between ultrasonic atomization parameters (amplitude, frequency, metal spill on vibrating surface) and obtained atomization results (average particle size, particle size distribution, atomization time). Utilizing numerical modeling as a methodology, especially the finite element method, the possibilities of using ultrasonic atomization as an instrument to determine properties of liquid metals were considered as an introduction to a series of real experiments. Modeling was applied to liquids with different properties, atomized at a chosen specific constant frequency and amplitude. The results of the simulation are in line with the current state of knowledge about ultrasonic atomization. However, in the existing studies available to the authors, there are no data that can be compared directly, but indirect comparisons confirmed the conclusions of the preliminary literature analysis. The relationship between viscosity and surface tension and the average size of the atomization processes obtained in the simulation of particles was demonstrated, thus providing a tool for the development of the presented concept: ultrasonic atomization as a research method. Research and simulation results led to the final conclusion: ultrasonic atomization can be applied to study the properties of liquid metals and this will be the subject of further research and experimentation.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Integration of circular economy principles into additive manufacturing (AM) has emerged as a critical strategy for addressing economic and environmental challenges associated with the high-cost, resource-intensive production of NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs). This review presents a comprehensive analysis of the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) technique as an advanced recycling approach for converting NiTi AM waste into high-quality feedstock. Furthermore, UPA demonstrates significant potential as a dual-function method, enabling both alloying and fine powder production within a single integrated process. AM processes, such as powder bed fusion-laser beam (PBF-LB), binder jetting, and direct energy deposition (DED), often result in substantial material losses, exacerbated by powder degradation phenomena including oxidation, particle morphology changes, and loss of flowability. While conventional atomization techniques, such as gas and plasma atomization, offer partial solutions for powder production, they are limited by significant energy inefficiencies, high capital investment requirements, and increased risks of contamination. Moreover, powders produced via gas atomization typically exhibit inferior quality compared to those generated by UPA, including lower sphericity and a higher prevalence of surface satellites. In contrast, the UPA system, a hybrid technique combining high-frequency ultrasonic vibrations and plasma melting, offers precise control over droplet formation through acoustic cavitation, Faraday wave instabilities, and rapid solidification, enabling the production of highly spherical, homogeneous, and contamination-minimized NiTi powders. Drawing on thermofluidic principles, vibrational mechanics, and metallurgical kinetics, this review systematically deconstructs the UPA mechanism, highlighting key phenomena such as resonance-induced cavitation dynamics, ultrasonic capillary wave collapse, and non-equilibrium solidification. Furthermore, it investigates contamination pathways specific to UPA and proposes strategies for impurity mitigation, including sonotrode design optimization, inert atmosphere refinement, and post-atomization conditioning. Experimental findings are analyzed to demonstrate the feasibility of achieving high sphericity (> 0.9), compositionally stable, and thermally responsive NiTi powders from recycled feedstock. Finally, the review outlines a roadmap for industrial-scale deployment, advocating the integration of machine learning and closed-loop recycling models to enhance process predictability, quality control, and resource efficiency. The insights presented herein position UPA as a transformative solution for enabling sustainable, high-performance NiTi powder regeneration within AM workflows, advancing the circular economy in advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Over recent years, ultrasonic atomization, especially with regard to liquid metals, has become an object of increased interest, mainly from industry, for additive manufacturing, but also from investigators, for research purposes. A strong correlation between the average particle size, distribution of particle sizes, and other process parameters like frequency and vibration amplitude was noted based on the analysis of available theoretical studies, simulations and experiments. The influence of parameters of the atomized fluid-like viscosity and surface tension on process parameters was also mentioned. The objective of this study is further research on the feasibility of using ultrasonic atomization to examine the properties of liquids, especially metals in liquid state. It attempts to close a gap in existing knowledge in searching for a new, possibly simple and cost-effective method to study the properties of liquid metals and further clarify the relationship between ultrasonic atomization parameters (amplitude, frequency, characteristics of metal being spilled on a vibrating surface) and obtained atomization results meant by average particle size and atomization time. Using numerical modeling (finite element method and computational fluid dynamics) as a methodology, combined with tests of using ultrasonic atomization as an instrument to determine properties of liquid metals, was considered as an introduction to a series of experiments. These tests were followed by real experiments that are also presented. At the first stage, numerical modeling was applied to a case of a specific liquid being spilled over a vibrating surface of different angles of inclination and specified, constant frequency and amplitude. The results of the simulation are in line with the current state of knowledge about ultrasonic atomization. Moreover, they can provide some more information on scalability, thus easing the comparison of the results of other experiments presented in the available literature. As a result, the relationship between fluid properties and the average size of atomized particles was demonstrated independently of the surface inclination angle. In the same way, the dependence of successful atomization on a sufficiently thin layer of a liquid was demonstrated. Thirdly, a correlation between the aforementioned layer thickness and the value of vibration amplitude has also been shown. Taking all the above into consideration, ultrasonic atomization can also be considered a research method and can be applied to study the properties of liquid metals. Further research, simulations and experimentation will be conducted to verify, develop and describe this method in full.

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing (AM) is a layer-by-layer process that makes the direct manufacturing of various industrial parts possible. This method facilitates the design and fabrication of complex industrial, advanced, and fine parts that are used in different industry sectors, such as aerospace, medicine, turbines, and jewelry, where the utilization of other fabrication techniques is difficult or impossible. This method is advantageous in terms of dimensional accuracy and fabrication speed. However, the parts fabricated by this method may suffer from faults such as anisotropy, micro-porosity, and defective joints. Metals like titanium, aluminum, stainless steels, superalloys, etc., have been used—in the form of powder or wire—as feed materials in the additive manufacturing of various parts. The main criterion that distinguishes different additive manufacturing processes from each other is the deposition method. With regard to this criterion, AM processes can be divided into four classes: local melting, sintering, sheet forming, and electrochemical methods. Parameters affecting the properties of the additive-manufactured part and the defects associated with an AM process determine the method by which a certain part should be manufactured. This study is a survey of different additive manufacturing processes, their mechanisms, capabilities, shortcomings, and the general properties of the parts manufactured by them.

Abstract:
Abstract The recent development of a novel family of power ultrasonic transducers with extensive radiating surfaces represents a step forward in the implementation of new airborne power ultrasonic (APU) technologies for drying process intensification at low temperature. These systems have been successfully used to assist drying of different products at laboratory level. This work deals with the development, integration, and testing of a new APU transducer with a stepped-grooved circular radiator as an initial step in scaling up the process and the results achieved in experiments of airborne atmospheric freeze-drying (AFD) of apples. The results confirm that ultrasound application leads to a significant intensification of the processes. The modeling shows that the increase of kinetic parameters was lower than those obtained with cylindrical transducers having the same electrical input. This fact is attributed to the treatment of greater volume.

Ultrasonic small scale flow reactors have found increasing popularity among researchers as they serve as a very useful platform for studying and controlling ultrasound mechanisms and effects. This has led to the use of these reactors for not only research purposes, but also various applications in biological, pharmaceutical and chemical processes mostly on laboratory and, in some cases, pilot scale. This review summarizes the state of the art of ultrasonic flow reactors and provides a guideline towards their design, characterization and application. Particular examples for ultrasound enhanced multiphase processes, spanning from immiscible fluid–fluid to fluid–solid systems, are provided. To conclude, challenges such as reactor efficiency and scalability are addressed.

From text 'presz2024ultrasonicatomizationas pages 6-7'.

Wojciech Presz, Rafał Szostak-Staropiętka, Anna Dziubińska, and Katarzyna Kołacz. Ultrasonic atomization as a method for testing material properties of liquid metals. Materials, 17:6109, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17246109, doi:10.3390/ma17246109. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt presents the Lang-type relationship between capillary wavelength and droplet size in ultrasonic atomization. The average or median droplet diameter is given by d = 0.34λ, where λ is the capillary wavelength. Combining this with the capillary-wave expression gives d = 0.34(8πσ/(ρf²))^(1/3), with σ denoting liquid surface tension, ρ liquid density, and f vibration frequency. Thus, droplet size increases with the cube root of surface tension and decreases with the cube root of density and the two-thirds power of frequency: d ∝ σ^(1/3)ρ^(−1/3)f^(−2/3). The numerical factor 0.34 is the reported proportionality constant relating average particle diameter to capillary wavelength. The excerpt notes that capillary-wave frequency is half the source forcing frequency, so the frequency convention should be checked when applying the formula. It also cautions that later studies found constants different from 0.34 and a wider range of values depending on the ultrasonic device; therefore, 0.34 is a useful initial or empirical estimate rather than an invariant universal constant.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'wong2022analysisofliquid pages 10-17'.

M Wong. Analysis of liquid atomization using ultrasonic waves. Unknown journal, 2022.

The excerpt gives Lang’s equation for the median droplet diameter in ultrasonic atomization as D = 0.34(8πT/(ρF²))^(1/3), where D is the median diameter of the atomization distribution, T is liquid surface tension in N/m, ρ is liquid density, and F is the applied excitation frequency in Hz. The equation is based on the observed proportionality between capillary wavelength and ultrasonic atomized droplet size. In proportional terms, droplet diameter increases with the cube root of surface tension, D ∝ T^(1/3), decreases with the cube root of density, D ∝ ρ^(-1/3), and decreases with the two-thirds power of excitation frequency, D ∝ F^(-2/3). Thus, higher surface tension produces larger predicted droplets, while higher liquid density or frequency produces smaller droplets. The numerical factor 0.34 is presented as Lang’s empirical proportionality coefficient in this formulation; the excerpt does not provide a separate derivation, uncertainty, or units for the coefficient.

The excerpt presents the wavelength relation used for ultrasonic capillary waves, attributed to Rayleigh’s modification of the earlier capillary-wave equation: λ = [8πT/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where T is surface tension, ρ is liquid density, and f is the forcing sound frequency. It then gives the Lang relationship between atomized droplet diameter and capillary wavelength as D = 0.34λ. Thus, the characteristic or median droplet diameter scales with the cube root of surface tension and inversely with the two-thirds power of both liquid density and excitation frequency: D = 0.34[8πT/(ρf²)]^(1/3). The proportionality constant 0.34 is an empirical coefficient connecting droplet diameter to capillary wavelength; it is dimensionless when both D and λ use the same length units. The excerpt also notes that experimentally reported diameter-to-wavelength or related frequency-based ratios commonly fall around 0.34–0.36. Consequently, increasing frequency or density reduces the predicted droplet size, while increasing surface tension increases it. The source specifically identifies D as the atomized droplet diameter, though the displayed passage does not separately define a statistical median beyond describing droplet diameter.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'kooij2019sizedistributionsof pages 1-2'.

Stefan Kooij, Alina Astefanei, Garry L. Corthals, and Daniel Bonn. Size distributions of droplets produced by ultrasonic nebulizers. Scientific Reports, Apr 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-42599-8, doi:10.1038/s41598-019-42599-8. This article has 179 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes Lang’s capillary-wave scaling for ultrasonic atomization. The capillary wavelength λ is determined by surface tension σ, liquid density ρ, wave frequency f, and, for finite liquid depth, the depth-dependent factor tanh(2πh/λ). For a sufficiently deep liquid layer, this factor approaches one, giving λ proportional to (σ/(ρf²))^(1/3). The nonlinear Faraday-wave frequency is f = F/2, where F is the nebulizer’s excitation frequency. Substitution yields the commonly cited median-droplet relation D50 = κλ = κ(8πσ/(ρF²))^(1/3). Thus, droplet size increases with surface tension, decreases with density, and decreases with excitation frequency according to an inverse two-thirds-power dependence: D50 ∝ σ^(1/3)ρ^(-1/3)F^(-2/3). Lang’s proportionality constant is κ = 0.34. In the cited original context, this value applies to the median droplet size of the number distribution; the article states that it subsequently uses D50 to denote the median particle size by volume. The paper also notes that measured κ values can differ somewhat among nebulizer types.

Consequently, droplet size scales as σ^(1/3), decreases as density^(−1/3), and decreases as frequency^(−2/3): d50 ≈ 0.34[8πσ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), subject to the frequency convention. The numerical proportionality constant 0.34 is the empirical/theoretical factor relating the median droplet diameter to the resonant capillary wavelength; it is not a separate dependence on surface tension or density.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Spraying various liquids (primarily aqueous solutions of various substances) is widely used in various technological processes. For most of them, high dispersibility and narrow droplet size distribution are essential. This facilitates ultrasonic spray technique. However, the higher the dispersity of droplets produced by ultrasonic spray, the lower the spray productivity. To solve this problem, we proposed a method of multistage spraying, consisting in generation of a large number of particles of large initial size (to ensure high productivity) and their subsequent destruction by propagation in a periodic ultrasonic field (to ensure small droplet sizes at high productivity). To experimentally determine the capabilities of this technique, a tubular emitter in the shape of a cylinder of stepped-variable cross-section was designed. Configuration of the ultrasonic field inside the emitter (22.2 kHz; 182 dB) implements three-stage spraying (the number of sputtering stages corresponds to the number of anti-nodes along the emitter axis). The effectiveness of proposed and developed technique suitable for generation of droplets sized less than 40 µm with performance exceeding the known ultrasonic spray techniques at least 10 times has been confirmed in the course of conducted research.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In this work, Porous copper foam samples were fabricated by a space-holder technique with water-atomized copper powder and sodium chloride (NaCl) particles in weight fractions ranging from 10 to 35 wt%. The powders were mechanically mixed at a 10:1 ball-to-powder ratio and 150 rpm for 2 h. The effects of space-holder content on the physical, mechanical, tribological, and electrochemical performance were systematically investigated. Increasing the NaCl fraction precisely controlled the total porosity, from 39.15% to 57.76%, and reduced the bulk density from 5.452 to 3.785 g/cm³. XRD and SEM analyses confirmed a single-phase FCC copper matrix and a structural transition from isolated pores to a highly interconnected open-cell network. Consequently, Vickers hardness, compressive yield strength, energy absorption capacity decreased from 52.12 to 29.23 HV, 18.25 to 1.65 MPa, and 35.73 to 10.46 MJ/m³, respectively, following a modified Gibson–Ashby model (R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                     = 0.95). Concurrently, the coefficient of friction and specific wear rate increased (reaching a maximum of 0.73 mm³/N·m under 15 N for 35 wt% NaCl) due to strut thinning and localized delamination. Electrochemical evaluation in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution revealed an optimization threshold for sample fabricated with 25 wt% NaCl, which exhibited the lowest corrosion rate of 0.918 mm/y, and the highest polarization resistance (Rp) of 267.28 Ω, due to a stable Cu
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O passive film. Exceeding this threshold at 30 and 35 wt% NaCl led to structural instability and stagnant electrolyte zones, accelerating corrosion kinetics. Overall, lower-porosity porous copper foam architectures offer superior structural energy absorption, whereas the 25 wt% NaCl configuration achieves an optimal balance between mechanical integrity and corrosion resistance.
                  </jats:p>

## pqac-00000008

From text 'szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 11-13'.

Rafał Szostak-Staropiętka, Wojciech Presz, Roksana Pawlic, Anna Dziubińska, and Katarzyna Kołacz. Influence of process parameters on the ultrasonic atomization efficiency and possibility of testing properties of liquid metals. Metrology, 5:39, Jul 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/metrology5030039, doi:10.3390/metrology5030039. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt identifies an onset vibration amplitude, rather than a critical acceleration: for a liquid with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m³, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, ultrasonic atomization required an amplitude of at least 8 µm. The initially measured converter amplitude was only about 2.8 µm, and atomization was unsuccessful; after the system was adjusted to reach 8 µm, atomization proceeded smoothly and was strongest at the vibrating-plate nodes. The excerpt does not provide a corresponding critical acceleration or a numerical maximum film thickness that can be atomized. It instead describes a qualitative thickness relationship. When the amplitude is too small, successive droplets form a patterned buildup layer whose thickness increases, while atomization does not begin, even though generator power rises. The conclusions state that atomization begins after the liquid’s spreading speed falls below a threshold. Atomization occurs first from the wavefront when its speed reaches a minimum, and then from the center when the liquid-layer thickness decreases below a certain value, in a direction perpendicular to the liquid surface. Thus, a thicker accumulating film is not necessarily atomized; successful atomization requires sufficient vibration amplitude and, locally, a sufficiently thin layer and low spreading speed. No maximum atomizable thickness is stated in these pages.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'song2021simulationofonset pages 8-11'.

Yu-Lin Song, Chih-Hsiao Cheng, Manoj Kumar Reddy, and Md Saikhul Islam. Simulation of onset of the capillary surface wave in the ultrasonic atomizer. Micromachines, 12:1146, Sep 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/mi12101146, doi:10.3390/mi12101146. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt identifies the Faraday-instability and ultrasonic-atomization onset threshold as approximately 0.38 µm vibration amplitude at a 500 kHz operating frequency. The COMSOL simulation found a minimum critical amplitude hcr = 0.38 µm, closely matching the experimentally measured 0.37 µm and the theoretical/numerical infinite-boundary prediction of 0.349 µm. At 0.36 µm, the amplitude remained below onset: no minimum Faraday wave formed and the fluid was not atomized, although the droplet distribution was non-uniform. At 0.38 µm, the Faraday wave grew within 300 periods, a 250 kHz subharmonic appeared, and the surface layer atomized. Higher amplitudes, such as 0.40 µm and above, enhanced the wave more rapidly and also atomized the surface. The excerpt does not provide a critical acceleration value, nor does it state a maximum atomizable film thickness. It only discusses a water-tank liquid domain and says that once the wave amplitude exceeds hcr with positive growth rate, the amplitude grows until surface tension can no longer sustain the vibration and the liquid breaks into drops. Therefore, this passage supports a threshold-amplitude relationship but does not establish how film thickness affects atomization success or specify a maximum film thickness.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'song2021simulationofonset pages 11-13'.

Yu-Lin Song, Chih-Hsiao Cheng, Manoj Kumar Reddy, and Md Saikhul Islam. Simulation of onset of the capillary surface wave in the ultrasonic atomizer. Micromachines, 12:1146, Sep 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/mi12101146, doi:10.3390/mi12101146. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt identifies the onset threshold in terms of capillary-surface displacement amplitude, not acceleration. At 500 kHz, onset was experimentally observed at he = 0.38 µm, compared with he = 0.36 µm where the tiny waves did not yet show the same onset behavior. Numerical analysis and linear Faraday-wave theory predicted a critical onset amplitude of hcr = 0.349 µm, indicating good agreement with the experiment. The passage does not provide a corresponding critical acceleration value, nor does it give a maximum atomizable film thickness. It states qualitatively that atomization increases as the vibrational amplitude of the capillary surface waves increases. Once the critical onset condition is reached, the Faraday-instability wave on the liquid surface can produce microdroplets in a single-frequency ultrasonic atomizer. The excerpt also notes a subharmonic-frequency condition at 250 kHz involving a finite lateral boundary condition, but it does not quantify how this changes the threshold. Therefore, the supplied pages support a threshold displacement-amplitude range near 0.35–0.38 µm and a positive relationship between amplitude and atomization success, while the requested maximum film thickness and acceleration threshold are not reported in this excerpt.

## pqac-00000011

From text 'song2021simulationofonset pages 4-6'.

Yu-Lin Song, Chih-Hsiao Cheng, Manoj Kumar Reddy, and Md Saikhul Islam. Simulation of onset of the capillary surface wave in the ultrasonic atomizer. Micromachines, 12:1146, Sep 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/mi12101146, doi:10.3390/mi12101146. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt identifies a Faraday-wave onset threshold at 500 kHz: the critical vibrational amplitude is 0.349 µm, corresponding to the neutral condition s = 0. Instability begins when the wave-growth rate becomes positive (s > 0); below this threshold, s < 0 indicates a stable liquid surface. If the 0.349 µm value is interpreted as displacement amplitude at 500 kHz, the corresponding sinusoidal acceleration is approximately 3.45 × 10^6 m/s², or about 3.5 × 10^5 g, although the excerpt itself does not explicitly report a critical acceleration. The modeled liquid depth was 1 mm, but this is a simulation parameter rather than an identified maximum film thickness that can be atomized. The excerpt does not provide a maximum atomizable film thickness or a quantitative relationship between film thickness and atomization success. It does indicate that once the standing capillary wave grows beyond the threshold and overcomes surface-tension constraints, atomization can occur. It also states that droplet diameter is proportional to the wavelength of the standing capillary waves, and that the surface-wave frequency is half the vibration frequency in the described subharmonic regime.

The excerpt identifies the onset threshold for Faraday instability and ultrasonic atomization as a minimum vibrational amplitude of 0.38 µm at an ultrasonic frequency of 500 kHz. The supplied pages do not establish a specific quantitative relationship between film thickness and atomization success, beyond noting that the onset amplitude is depth-dependent. ## pqac-00000013

From text 'song2021simulationofonset pages 2-4'.

Yu-Lin Song, Chih-Hsiao Cheng, Manoj Kumar Reddy, and Md Saikhul Islam. Simulation of onset of the capillary surface wave in the ultrasonic atomizer. Micromachines, 12:1146, Sep 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/mi12101146, doi:10.3390/mi12101146. This article has 6 citations.

The excerpt defines the onset of Faraday instability as occurring when the vertical vibration amplitude reaches a threshold, but it does not provide a numerical threshold amplitude or critical acceleration. It introduces a minimum capillary-wave amplitude, hcr, obtained by perturbation theory and dependent on liquid properties including viscosity, density, surface tension, and wave frequency. For finite liquid depth, the initial critical amplitude depends on the liquid depth; for an effectively infinite-depth condition, onset is associated with the capillary-surface energy reaching the minimum required for atomization. Under low surface-viscosity and weak-boundary conditions, the capillary-wave amplitude is reported as approximately half the exciting vibration amplitude, with a π/4 phase shift. The excerpt does not state a maximum atomizable film thickness. It only indicates that liquid depth or film thickness affects the critical onset amplitude: finite-depth conditions require considering depth, while the deep-water approximation applies when wavelength is much smaller than liquid depth. Therefore, the relationship described is that thickness/depth influences whether the required instability threshold is reached, but no explicit maximum thickness or quantitative atomization-success criterion is given here.

Abstract:
In an era of rapid technological development, ultrasound technology is being used in a wide range of industries. The use of ultrasound technology in fruit and vegetable processing to improve production efficiency and product quality has been an important research topic. The cleaning of whole fresh fruits and vegetables is an important part of fruit and vegetable processing. This paper discusses the development process of components of the ultrasonic equipment, the application of ultrasonic technology in fruit and vegetable cleaning, and the research advances in ultrasonic cleaning technology. Moreover, the feasibility of ultrasonication of fruits and vegetables for cleaning from the perspectives of microbial inactivation, commodity storage, and sensory analysis were discussed. Finally, the paper identified the inevitable disadvantages of cavitation noise, erosion, and tissue damage in fruit and vegetable processing and points out the future directions of ultrasonic fruit and vegetable cleaning technology.

Rafał Szostak-Staropiętka, Wojciech Presz, Roksana Pawlic, Anna Dziubińska, and Katarzyna Kołacz. Influence of process parameters on the ultrasonic atomization efficiency and possibility of testing properties of liquid metals. Metrology, 5:39, Jul 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/metrology5030039, doi:10.3390/metrology5030039. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not report a maximum mass flow rate, throughput in kg/s, or a demonstrated throughput specifically for molten metals. It states only that liquid delivery was tested from one droplet per second up to a continuous stream through a calibrated 2 mm orifice. The results indicate that atomization capacity is constrained by ultrasonic amplitude and liquid properties rather than flow rate alone. For the tested liquid, with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m3, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, an amplitude of at least 8 µm was required to initiate atomization. When drops were supplied while amplitude was insufficient, liquid accumulated as a patterned film on the sonotrode plate; increasing feed increased film thickness and generator power, but did not necessarily initiate atomization or cause the liquid to drain. In the high-viscosity case, added liquid similarly thickened the buildup layer, with only minimal frequency change and increased power consumption. Once ultrasound was switched off, the accumulated film spread and flowed downward. Thus, the excerpt supports a qualitative relationship: feed rate above the atomization capacity causes film-thickness buildup and higher power demand, while sufficient amplitude is necessary for sustained atomization. A numerical maximum throughput cannot be derived from these pages.

The excerpt does not report a maximum mass flow rate or a quantified throughput for ultrasonic atomization of molten metals. In the experiment, liquid delivery was varied from one 2 mm droplet per second up to a continuous stream, but no corresponding mass-flow measurements, maximum sustainable feed rate, or atomization-capacity limit are provided. The results do indicate that atomization depends strongly on the liquid-film thickness on the sonotrode plate: atomization begins depending on the thickness of the liquid layer and proceeds fastest in the thinnest regions. Thus, increasing flow may increase the amount of liquid supplied beyond the rate that the vibrating surface can atomize, causing a thicker residual film and reducing complete atomization unless the plate area, vibration conditions, or drainage are adjusted. The study estimated process efficiency from the area of liquid remaining on the vibrating surface, rather than from mass throughput. For the simulated single-droplet case, changing the plate inclination from 30° to 60° changed the remaining liquid fraction only modestly, from 48.2% to 50.9%, suggesting that inclination was not the principal capacity control under those simplified conditions. A maximum throughput would require additional experimental data relating feed mass rate, film thickness, vibration amplitude/frequency, and the fraction converted to droplets.

A horizontal vibrating surface may increase heat transfer from the liquid metal to the sonotrode, potentially changing the characteristics of the vibrating stack. By contrast, tilting the surface is proposed to direct the atomized stream and make liquid-metal spillage easier. The excerpt explicitly states that easier spillage influences atomization efficiency and warns that excessive accumulation can stop atomization altogether. Thus, the implied relationship is that throughput is constrained by the ability of the sonotrode plate to maintain a suitable liquid layer and continuously remove atomized material: increasing feed beyond the plate's drainage or atomization capacity would increase accumulation/film thickness, reduce effective operation, and potentially halt the process.
