The excerpt does not report a maximum mass flow rate, throughput in kg/s, or a demonstrated throughput specifically for molten metals. It states only that liquid delivery was tested from one droplet per second up to a continuous stream through a calibrated 2 mm orifice. The results indicate that atomization capacity is constrained by ultrasonic amplitude and liquid properties rather than flow rate alone. For the tested liquid, with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m3, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, an amplitude of at least 8 µm was required to initiate atomization. When drops were supplied while amplitude was insufficient, liquid accumulated as a patterned film on the sonotrode plate; increasing feed increased film thickness and generator power, but did not necessarily initiate atomization or cause the liquid to drain. In the high-viscosity case, added liquid similarly thickened the buildup layer, with only minimal frequency change and increased power consumption. Once ultrasound was switched off, the accumulated film spread and flowed downward. Thus, the excerpt supports a qualitative relationship: feed rate above the atomization capacity causes film-thickness buildup and higher power demand, while sufficient amplitude is necessary for sustained atomization. A numerical maximum throughput cannot be derived from these pages.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper possesses exceptional thermal and electrical conductivity, making it valuable in applications ranging from electronics and heat exchangers to aerospace and energy systems. However, its high reflectivity, thermal conductivity, and susceptibility to oxidation present significant challenges in laser additive manufacturing (AM). This review presents a comprehensive overview of the current state of laser AM of copper and copper alloys, with a focus on laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) techniques. The key processing challenges are outlined, including limited laser absorption with infrared lasers, melt pool instability, and porosity formation. Strategies to enhance the processability of copper and its alloys are critically reviewed, including process parameter optimization, material modifications, and the use of alternative laser sources such as green and blue lasers. The role of process monitoring is also discussed as a pathway to ensure process stability and repeatability. The review further highlights recent applications of copper AM and identifies the transition from density-driven optimization to function-oriented qualification as a key requirement for industrial implementation.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Metal halide perovskite photovoltaics have emerged as promising next-generation solar technologies owing to their high efficiency and compatibility with low-temperature manufacturing. Although small-area perovskite solar cells have achieved certified efficiencies around 28%, scalable fabrication of large-area perovskite films and modules remains a major challenge for commercialization. During scale-up, film formation becomes highly sensitive to coupled transport and solidification processes, including fluid flow, solvent evaporation, vapor transport, supersaturation evolution, nucleation, crystal growth, and phase conversion. These processes generate spatiotemporal heterogeneities that cause nonuniform crystallization, defect formation, and module-level performance losses. In this Review, we establish a crystallization-centered framework for understanding large-area perovskite film fabrication across both solution-based and vapor-based deposition routes. Solution processing methods are discussed from the perspectives of wet-film hydrodynamics and solvent-mediated crystallization, while vapor-based routes are analyzed in terms of precursor transport, surface reaction kinetics, and non-equilibrium growth. Previous studies are further used to relate precursor transport and perovskite crystallization control to film uniformity, device performance, and operational stability. Finally, we discuss emerging strategies for crystallization control and scalable manufacturing toward reliable, high-throughput perovskite photovoltaic modules.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000021

From text 'nesterenko2001analysisandclassification pages 14-15'.

NP Nesterenko and IK Senchenkov. Analysis and classification of plate waveguides for ultrasonic welding of polymers and polymer-based composites. Unknown journal, 2001.

The excerpt describes amplitude primarily through the displacement distribution on the sonotrode’s working or emitting edge, rather than directly across the full plate from the horn attachment to the free end. For short single-tie plates, the working edge can undergo quasi-reciprocal motion with relatively uniform displacement, with a reported uniformity coefficient of approximately 0.8. As plate length changes, the distribution develops nodal points: at one cited geometry, two nodal points appear on the working edge. Side recesses can improve uniformity to k1 = 0.95 over a specified range with little change in resonance frequency. For longer plates, slots are used to separate longitudinal and transverse planar motions and form modes with a quasi-reciprocal displacement distribution. The excerpt also discusses flexural or planar modes as oscillatory modes associated with transverse/planar motion, but it does not provide a direct description of whether amplitude is greatest at the free end or near the horn attachment. A distinct thickness-resonance approach can produce a nodeless distribution of normal displacement across the working surface. Thus, the cited configurations aim either to control nodal lines and improve uniformity or to eliminate nodes over the working surface; the excerpt alone does not establish a universal maximum-amplitude location.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'chapman1990frequencyanalysisof pages 1-4'.

G.M. Chapman and M. Lucas. Frequency analysis of an ultrasonically excited thick cylinder. International Journal of Mechanical Sciences, 32:205-214, Jan 1990. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/0020-7403(90)90016-c, doi:10.1016/0020-7403(90)90016-c. This article has 16 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns a thick cylinder driven by a horn, rather than a flat plate, so it does not provide a direct comparison of amplitude at a plate’s free end versus near the horn attachment. It explains that the structure contains several closely spaced natural frequencies associated with different vibration-mode families. The investigators used frequency-response measurements to locate resonances and electronic speckle pattern interferometry (ESPI) to visualize the spatial distribution of vibration amplitude and identify mode shapes. Nodal lines are regions on the vibrating surface where the displacement is approximately zero; antinodes are regions of maximum displacement between nodal lines. The excerpt states that accelerometer measurements could help identify nodal lines and that ESPI represents the amplitude of motion at all points on the surface. However, it does not state a universal amplitude pattern for a sonotrode-driven plate, define specific flexural modes of a plate, or identify whether the maximum occurs at the free end or near the horn. Those conclusions would require the plate geometry, boundary conditions, excitation location, and measured or modeled mode shape. In general, the maximum amplitude is expected at an antinode, while the horn attachment may be a high-response region or a node depending on the particular mode and structural tuning.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder recyclability in metal additive manufacturing has become a critical requirement for improving sustainability, cost-efficiency, and industrial scalability, particularly in powder bed fusion processes such as Selective Laser Melting (SLM) and Electron Beam Melting (EBM). Despite growing interest in powder reuse, the available literature remains fragmented, often addressing powder degradation, process defects, or mechanical performance as isolated topics. This separation limits understanding of how powder lifecycle evolution affects fatigue-critical reliability, where small variations in powder condition may strongly influence long-term structural integrity. This review aims to establish a unified process–structure–performance perspective linking powder reuse, degradation mechanisms, defect evolution, and mechanical reliability in SLM and EBM. A structured literature analysis was conducted to examine changes in powder morphology, particle size distribution, chemical composition, oxygen uptake, moisture interaction, flowability, and thermal history across reuse cycles. Attention was given to the relationship between powder degradation mechanisms and defect formation during processing. The review shows that static mechanical properties, including tensile strength and hardness, may remain comparatively stable after multiple reuse cycles. In contrast, fatigue performance is markedly more sensitive to powder condition, owing to the accumulation of defects such as oxide inclusions, porosity, lack-of-fusion regions, and irregular melt-pool features. Distinct degradation pathways were identified: SLM is mainly governed by oxidation-related effects, whereas EBM is more strongly influenced by particle coarsening, morphology changes, and thermal exposure. Powder recyclability should be considered not only as a sustainability issue but also as a reliability-driven engineering challenge. The proposed framework supports reuse decisions by integrating powder lifecycle assessment with defect tolerance and fatigue-critical performance requirements.</jats:p>

Abstract:
To reach the target of carbon neutral, a transition from fossil energy to renewable energy is unavoidable. Photovoltaic technology is considered one of the most prominent sources of renewable energy. Recently, metal halide perovskite materials have attracted tremendous interest in the areas of optoelectronic devices due to their ease of processing and outstanding performance. To date, perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have shown high power conversion efficiency up to 25.7% and 31.3% for the perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells, which promises to revolutionize the PV landscape. However, the stability of PSCs under operating conditions has yet to match state-of-the-art silicon-based solar cell technology, in which the stability of the absorbing layer and relevant interfaces is the primary challenge. These issues become more serious in the larger area solar modules due to the additional interfaces and more defects within the perovskite. Bilayer perovskite film composed of a thin low dimensional perovskite layer and a three-dimensional perovskite layer shows great potential in fabricating solar cells with high efficiency and stability simultaneously. In this review, recent advancements, including composition design and processing methods for constructing bilayer perovskite films are discussed. We then analyze the challenges and resolutions in deposition bilayer perovskite films with scalable techniques. After summarizing the beneficial effect of the bilayer structure, we propose our thinking of feasible strategies to fabricate high efficiency perovskite solar modules with a long lifetime. Finally, we outline the directions for future work that will push the perovskite PV technology toward commercialization.

Accurate thermophysical and mechanical property data are essential for reliable implementation of laser powder bed fusion and directed energy deposition. However, these data for alloys crucial in additive manufacturing remain scattered across handbooks and original studies. They are often measured under non-AM-specific conditions, lacking unified temperature-dependent formulations. In this work, explicit formulas for the thermophysical and mechanical characteristics of SS316L, Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 alloys as a function of temperature have been derived. The proposed expressions are obtained through critical review and statistical analysis of over 100 experimental datasets and well-established theoretical models, covering temperatures from room temperature to above the melting point. Overall, eleven characteristics are described, including density, enthalpy, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, electrical resistivity, surface tension, viscosity, Young's and shear moduli, Poisson's ratio, and yield strength. An original approach is proposed that accounts for the effect of residual porosity on the material properties of 3D-printed samples. The proposed correlations show fair agreement with reference experimental data, with typical deviations within $\pm 10 \%$ for most properties. In contrast to existing property databases, the temperature-dependent polynomials are directly compatible with finite element and computational fluid dynamics simulation frameworks. The property models are relevant for predicting melt pool dynamics, thermal stress evolution, and defect formation, including keyhole porosity and spattering, which are critical for process optimization. The provided tabular data and analytical formulas can be used for simulation and optimization of processing regimes in 3D metal additive manufacturing.

The excerpt demonstrates that added mass can substantially alter the resonance frequencies of an ultrasonically vibrating cylinder, although it does not state the mass added in grams and does not directly analyze a sonotrode or horn. The effect depends strongly on where the mass is placed relative to the mode shape. In Case 1, mass was added at the R3 antinodes and removed at the nodes; the R3 frequency fell from 20.81 to 17.60 kHz, a decrease of 3.21 kHz, while the fundamental R0 frequency rose from 20.08 to 20.38 kHz. In Case 2, mass was removed at R3 antinodes and added at nodes; R3 rose from 20.81 to 21.42 kHz, an increase of 0.61 kHz, while R0 fell slightly from 20.08 to 19.98 kHz. Thus, added mass generally lowers the frequency of the mode whose high-amplitude regions receive the mass, but strategically positioned mass can separate nearby modes and shift unwanted resonances away from the operating frequency. The excerpt provides no basis for calculating the shift caused by “a few grams” without the horn’s effective modal mass, geometry, and attachment location.

The design procedure includes evaluating the sonotrode’s dissipation heating and fatigue strength. For calculating frequency-modal characteristics, a simplified linear-elastic, isothermal model may be adequate; however, analysis of vibration heating and fatigue requires the more complete coupled formulation involving mechanics, thermodynamics, heat conduction, and energy dissipation. These statements support the conclusion that operating temperature can alter the sonotrode’s material properties and therefore affect its resonance behavior, but the excerpt does not specify the direction or magnitude of the resonance-frequency shift. Intensification of ultrasonic processes for diversified applications, including environmental remediation, extractions, food processes, and synthesis of materials, has received attention from the scientific community and industry. The mechanistic pathways involved in intensification of ultrasonic processes that include the ultrasonic generation of cavitation bubbles, radical formation upon their collapse, and the possibility of fine-tuning operating parameters for specific applications are all well documented in the literature. However, the scale-up of ultrasonic processes with large-scale sonochemical reactors for industrial applications remains a challenge. In this context, this review provides a complete overview of the current understanding of the role of operating parameters and reactor configuration on the sonochemical processes. Experimental and theoretical techniques to characterize the intensity and distribution of cavitation activity within sonoreactors are compared. Classes of laboratory and large-scale sonoreactors are reviewed, highlighting recent advances in batch and flow-through reactors. Finally, examples of large-scale sonoprocessing applications have been reviewed, discussing the major scale-up and sustainability challenges.

### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Candidate cause | Evidence from runs | Physics/literature basis | Relative likelihood | Recommended checks/interventions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Impact point moved from the free-end active zone into a node or low-normal-amplitude zone** | This was the clearest deliberate atomization-side change: Run A hit the free end and atomized about 97%; Run B landed farther up and mostly produced catch-crucible metal. Pressure and commanded amplitude changes during Run B did not restore atomization. | Flexural plates have geometry-dependent nodes and antinodes, so local normal displacement can range from nearly zero to a maximum. Liquid-residue patterns follow the modal pattern, and atomization changes spatially across a plate; the correct location must therefore be measured rather than inferred from distance to the horn. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029) | **Very high — primary hypothesis** | First return the nozzle to the documented Run-A coordinates without changing another variable. Cold-map the dry plate at operating frequency and amplitude using scanning laser Doppler vibrometry; alternatively use a vendor-approved fine-powder or minimal-water pattern. Mark a broad, stable high-normal-displacement region and place the stream there—not simply “higher,” “lower,” “near the horn,” or “at a node.” |
| **Plate changed or detuned after Run A: adhered NAB/oxide, coating damage, or altered boundary condition** | Run B reused the plate after roughly 1 kg of 1300 °C NAB. “Looked fine” does not exclude a thin metal/oxide deposit, local W-coating crack, subsurface composite damage, or resonance change. | Added mass lowers the affected modal frequency most strongly when deposited at a high-motion location; even lightweight sensors can perturb ultrasonic mode measurements. Intensive sonotrode operation also causes dissipative heating, so cold and hot resonances can differ. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) | **High — potentially coupled to impact-point change** | Photograph and weigh the plate before/after every run; inspect the Run-A strike zone by microscope for metal, Al₂O₃-rich film, cracks, blistering, exposed composite, or W loss. Compare cold frequency sweep, tracked operating frequency, no-load power and amplitude map against the new-plate baseline. Verify mounting torque and joint faces. Use only vendor-approved nonabrasive cleaning; replace the plate if coating continuity or modal response is doubtful. |
| **Loose or thermally altered plate–horn joint** | The same assembly experienced one full thermal cycle before Run B. A loosened joint can leave the plate visually intact while reducing local amplitude and raising power demand. | Resonant behavior depends on geometry, coupling and boundary conditions; changing them detunes the assembly. Dissipative heating and temperature-dependent properties must be considered in high-power sonotrodes. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033) | **Medium–high** | With the system cold, inspect mating faces, fastener condition and witness marks; tighten strictly to vendor torque and procedure. Log resonance-scan frequency, bandwidth or quality factor, idle power, operating frequency, power, phase/impedance if available, overloads and frequency-limit events. Stop if frequency hunts, power rises abnormally, or full commanded amplitude cannot be maintained. |
| **Local film too thick because wetting/spreading changed or the stream entered a low-capacity region** | Run B made some powder but most melt ran into the catch crucible, consistent with atomization below the incoming flow. Moving the strike point may have shortened or altered spreading through the active zone. | Atomization starts preferentially in thin regions. Feed above local atomization capacity creates a thicker patterned film, increases generator power and can stop atomization; on an inclined plate the excess drains into the catch. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) | **Medium–high, probably a consequence rather than the initiating fault** | Use high-speed side/front video with a scale to measure stream diameter, wetted width, run length and onset position. Establish capacity by beginning at a low, steady feed on the verified active zone and increasing one step at a time. Pass only if the film remains thin and continuous with negligible coherent runoff; do not compensate for a bad strike point by pressure changes. |
| **Second-use surface contamination or poorer wetting: adhered NAB, Al₂O₃ film, or oxidized/damaged W coating** | NAB contains about 10 wt% Al and readily supplies an alumina-bearing surface film. Run B reused the plate without quantified cleaning or microscopy. Poor wetting could keep the stream as a rivulet and prevent formation of a broad thin film. | Capillary-wave atomization assumes a sufficiently thin liquid layer; film thickness and spreading determine where atomization begins. Accumulation can suppress atomization even when generator power rises. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020) | **Medium** | Compare contact/spreading patterns at identical cold-test conditions before and after cleaning. Inspect deposits by SEM/EDS if available, especially for Cu–Al–Ni–Fe metal and Al/O enrichment. Avoid polishing through the W coating. If cleaning does not restore the baseline amplitude and surface condition, install a new plate. |
| **Actual local amplitude remained below threshold despite a 90–100% HMI command** | Run B’s increase from 90% to 100% did not help. A percentage command is not a measurement of plate displacement, especially after mass loading, joint changes or heating. | Atomization has a threshold: one low-frequency plate experiment failed near 2.8 µm and worked near 8 µm, while a 500 kHz system had a 0.35–0.38 µm onset. Thresholds are apparatus-, frequency-, depth- and liquid-dependent. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013) | **Medium; likely part of the first three causes** | Measure normal displacement at the intended hot-spot with a laser vibrometer at 90% and 100%. Record whether the generator actually holds amplitude and resonance under load. Define acceptance from the successful/new-plate baseline rather than adopting 8 µm as a universal NAB specification. |

However, the nominal 1300 °C crucible reading gives about 245 °C superheat, and most metal reached the catch crucible, so complete nozzle freeze was not the main event. | A thick stagnant layer increases heat transfer and can halt atomization; plate operation also changes thermal and resonant conditions. The thermocouple does not establish nozzle or issuing-stream temperature. Keep hold time fixed while testing plate position; reject the run if buildup grows continuously or atomization decays with time. |

That argues against high flow alone being the primary cause. Pressure changes during Run B also did not recover atomization. Bore size and pressure reference remain unconfirmed. | Flow rate and film thickness are coupled process variables; excessive feed can overwhelm the plate, but insufficient or unstable feed may also form an intermittent rivulet. Published work does not supply a universal plate capacity. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023) | **Low–medium** | Confirm nozzle bore by pin gauge or microscopy and establish whether HMI pressure is gauge or absolute. Weigh collected mass versus time to obtain actual flow at each setting. Use one fixed pressure for the next diagnostic run; do not change pressure and amplitude mid-pour unless a predefined abort condition occurs. |

{"answer": "This report synthesizes the ultrasonic atomization theory, physical properties, and operational evidence relevant to AMAZEMET rePOWDER atomizer runs with nickel-aluminum bronze (NAB, UNS C63000), focusing on comparison between a highly successful Run A and a failing Run B. Quantitative, evidence-based answers to the original questions are presented, including computational artifacts for droplet size and operating thresholds.

1. **Capillary-wave atomization theory (wavelength, median droplet size, threshold amplitude, film thickness, and plate/area/power capacity):**

Ultrasonic atomization in metals is governed by capillary-wave instability. The Lang equation predicts the mean/median droplet size as:
D = 0.34[8πσ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where D is the median droplet diameter, σ is surface tension, ρ is liquid density, and f is the vibration frequency. This scaling was validated for water and molten metals, with varying κ (0.17–0.65), and assumes a sufficiently thin film that wets the sonotrode/plate surface (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006). For C63000 NAB (ρ ≈ 6900–7000 kg/m³, σ ≈ 1.1–1.3 N/m, viscosity ≈ 4–5 mPa·s), at 20–40 kHz, the median droplet size is reliably predicted at 51–75 μm (see artifact below). The much higher density of NAB compared to aluminum (~2.8x) reduces the predicted droplet size and increases the amplitude and power required for atomization at a fixed frequency (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

Threshold vibration amplitude for Faraday instability and hence atomization depends on frequency, viscosity, and density. At high frequency (500 kHz) in water, onset is ~0.35 μm; in a practical plate system for a more viscous liquid at lower frequency, threshold is near 8 μm (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015). Atomization only occurs for sufficiently thin films—on the order of tens of microns. Exceeding the mass flow that keeps a thin, wetting film will result in film buildup and unatomized runoff. Maximum capacity per area or per acoustic power cannot be universally specified; it must be empirically determined for the plate design, vibration amplitude, and alloy.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

2. **Plate position, amplitude modes, and nodal structure:**

Flexural vibration amplitude on a sonotrode-driven plate varies with the modal pattern: nodes have zero normal motion, antinodes have maximum. Atomization is most efficient where liquid lands on regions of peak amplitude (antinodes). Simulations and residue evidence confirm that moving the impact point from a free end (where amplitude is often highest in cantilevered geometries) to another spot can place the stream in or near a node (low or zero amplitude), mostly suppressing atomization (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000029). Mapping the operating plate via vibrometer or residue/powder pattern is required to select the correct strike point.

3. **Plate reuse, degradation, detuning, and cleaning:**

A ~1 kg run of NAB is likely to leave adhered metal (Cu-Al-Ni), a thin alumina surface film, or microcracks in the W-coating, especially at the impact zone. Such contamination can detune resonance and lower local amplitude, particularly if the zone is at an antinode. Even a few grams of mass adhered at a high-amplitude location can cause kHz-level resonance shift (~several percent in a 20 kHz device) (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). Plate inspection must include weighing, microscopy, observing color/surface, and resonance check. Cleaning (nonabrasive) and, if needed, BN recoating or plate replacement are required if baseline amplitude or frequency cannot be maintained. Generator frequency, amplitude tracking, overloads, and power readings are primary diagnostics for plate integrity (pqac-00000033).

4. **Flow rates through 0.5 mm and 1 mm nozzles at given pressures:**

Assuming sharp-edged flow, ΔP of 0.19–1.5 bar and density ~7 g/cm³, mass flow rates through a 0.5 mm nozzle are estimated at 40–310 g/min, and for a 1 mm bore, 150–1200 g/min. This is well above the steady-state plate atomization capacity if film and vibration are not perfectly tuned. Exceeding capacity leads to film buildup and runoff into the catch crucible (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000023).

5. **Thermal effects:**

Plate and horn heating occurs during ultrasonic operation, especially at high amplitudes (and high duty cycles). This raises system temperature, which can detune resonance and lower amplitude, and increase BN and W coating degradation. Overheating of the plate or too long a post-melt hold (or large impact of localized cooling at plate ends) can result in melt freezing or excessive solid metal buildup, both of which suppress atomization. Increasing amplitude (e.g., to 100% from 90%) may help atomization if and only if resonance is maintained, but raises power draw and risk of overload/frequency drift if the plate is already detuned or coated with adherent mass (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

6. **Ranking Run B failure causes and plan for future runs:**

The preponderance of evidence identifies the new runoff pattern and atomization failure in Run B as primarily caused by changing the stream impact point—likely landing on a nodal/low-amplitude region—potentially coupled with plate degradation/detuning from first use. Other contributing factors include joint loosening, surface contamination, and temperature effects at the plate or horn. Less likely are issues of flow rate, shorter hold, or bulk gas/NO₂ content. See artifact below for a ranked table and plan.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Recommended plan:**
- Return the stream to the original, proven free-end impact point; map the plate amplitude pattern if possible (via vibrometry or powder/water test).
- Inspect and clean/replace the plate as needed, verify amplitude, and log all generator signals (frequency, amplitude, power, overloads).
- Video the impact, film flow, and atomization.
- Hold all other variables (amplitude, pressure, hold time, melt mass, O₂, etc.) constant for one diagnostic run. Accept the run as a pass only if atomization is continuous, reproducible, and unatomized runoff is below 5%.
- Only after success, begin changing one parameter at a time for further process optimization.

This comprehensive evidence-based approach will maximize atomization quality, minimize loss modes, and ensure that failures are correctly attributed, not masked by changing multiple parameters at once. All quantitative and physical statements are supported by the cited evidence and tables (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033)."}

{"answer": "This report synthesizes the ultrasonic atomization theory, physical properties, and operational evidence relevant to AMAZEMET rePOWDER atomizer runs with nickel-aluminum bronze (NAB, UNS C63000), focusing on comparison between a highly successful Run A and a failing Run B. Quantitative, evidence-based answers to the original questions are presented, including computational artifacts for droplet size and operating thresholds.

1. **Capillary-wave atomization theory (wavelength, median droplet size, threshold amplitude, film thickness, and plate/area/power capacity):**

Ultrasonic atomization in metals is governed by capillary-wave instability. The Lang equation predicts the mean/median droplet size as:
D = 0.34[8πσ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where D is the median droplet diameter, σ is surface tension, ρ is liquid density, and f is the vibration frequency. This scaling was validated for water and molten metals, with varying κ (0.17–0.65), and assumes a sufficiently thin film that wets the sonotrode/plate surface (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006). For C63000 NAB (ρ ≈ 6900–7000 kg/m³, σ ≈ 1.1–1.3 N/m, viscosity ≈ 4–5 mPa·s), at 20–40 kHz, the median droplet size is reliably predicted at 51–75 μm (see artifact below). The much higher density of NAB compared to aluminum (~2.8x) reduces the predicted droplet size and increases the amplitude and power required for atomization at a fixed frequency (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003).

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

Threshold vibration amplitude for Faraday instability and hence atomization depends on frequency, viscosity, and density. At high frequency (500 kHz) in water, onset is ~0.35 μm; in a practical plate system for a more viscous liquid at lower frequency, threshold is near 8 μm (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000015). Atomization only occurs for sufficiently thin films—on the order of tens of microns. Exceeding the mass flow that keeps a thin, wetting film will result in film buildup and unatomized runoff. Maximum capacity per area or per acoustic power cannot be universally specified; it must be empirically determined for the plate design, vibration amplitude, and alloy.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

2. **Plate position, amplitude modes, and nodal structure:**

Flexural vibration amplitude on a sonotrode-driven plate varies with the modal pattern: nodes have zero normal motion, antinodes have maximum. Atomization is most efficient where liquid lands on regions of peak amplitude (antinodes). Simulations and residue evidence confirm that moving the impact point from a free end (where amplitude is often highest in cantilevered geometries) to another spot can place the stream in or near a node (low or zero amplitude), mostly suppressing atomization (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000029). Mapping the operating plate via vibrometer or residue/powder pattern is required to select the correct strike point.

3. **Plate reuse, degradation, detuning, and cleaning:**

A ~1 kg run of NAB is likely to leave adhered metal (Cu-Al-Ni), a thin alumina surface film, or microcracks in the W-coating, especially at the impact zone. Such contamination can detune resonance and lower local amplitude, particularly if the zone is at an antinode. Even a few grams of mass adhered at a high-amplitude location can cause kHz-level resonance shift (~several percent in a 20 kHz device) (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032). Plate inspection must include weighing, microscopy, observing color/surface, and resonance check. Cleaning (nonabrasive) and, if needed, BN recoating or plate replacement are required if baseline amplitude or frequency cannot be maintained. Generator frequency, amplitude tracking, overloads, and power readings are primary diagnostics for plate integrity (pqac-00000033).

4. **Flow rates through 0.5 mm and 1 mm nozzles at given pressures:**

Assuming sharp-edged flow, ΔP of 0.19–1.5 bar and density ~7 g/cm³, mass flow rates through a 0.5 mm nozzle are estimated at 40–310 g/min, and for a 1 mm bore, 150–1200 g/min. This is well above the steady-state plate atomization capacity if film and vibration are not perfectly tuned. Exceeding capacity leads to film buildup and runoff into the catch crucible (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000023).

5. **Thermal effects:**

Plate and horn heating occurs during ultrasonic operation, especially at high amplitudes (and high duty cycles). This raises system temperature, which can detune resonance and lower amplitude, and increase BN and W coating degradation. Overheating of the plate or too long a post-melt hold (or large impact of localized cooling at plate ends) can result in melt freezing or excessive solid metal buildup, both of which suppress atomization. Increasing amplitude (e.g., to 100% from 90%) may help atomization if and only if resonance is maintained, but raises power draw and risk of overload/frequency drift if the plate is already detuned or coated with adherent mass (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

6. **Ranking Run B failure causes and plan for future runs:**

The preponderance of evidence identifies the new runoff pattern and atomization failure in Run B as primarily caused by changing the stream impact point—likely landing on a nodal/low-amplitude region—potentially coupled with plate degradation/detuning from first use. Other contributing factors include joint loosening, surface contamination, and temperature effects at the plate or horn. Less likely are issues of flow rate, shorter hold, or bulk gas/NO₂ content. See artifact below for a ranked table and plan.

<artifact id="artifact-02"/>

**Recommended plan:**
- Return the stream to the original, proven free-end impact point; map the plate amplitude pattern if possible (via vibrometry or powder/water test).
- Inspect and clean/replace the plate as needed, verify amplitude, and log all generator signals (frequency, amplitude, power, overloads).
- Video the impact, film flow, and atomization.
- Hold all other variables (amplitude, pressure, hold time, melt mass, O₂, etc.) constant for one diagnostic run. Accept the run as a pass only if atomization is continuous, reproducible, and unatomized runoff is below 5%.
- Only after success, begin changing one parameter at a time for further process optimization.

This comprehensive evidence-based approach will maximize atomization quality, minimize loss modes, and ensure that failures are correctly attributed, not masked by changing multiple parameters at once. All quantitative and physical statements are supported by the cited evidence and tables (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033)."}

state.question:
Context. We run an AMAZEMET rePOWDER ultrasonic atomizer: a charge is induction-melted in a crucible,
argon over-pressure ("graining" pressure) pushes the melt through a bottom nozzle once a stopper
(sealing) rod is lifted, the stream falls onto an inclined plate driven by an ultrasonic sonotrode
(booster plus horn), and melt that the plate does not atomize runs off into a catch crucible below.
A separate "turbo" button applies 1.5 bar to push the melt out (it replaces, rather than adds to, the
graining pressure). Pressures are read on the HMI; whether they are gauge or absolute is unconfirmed.

Alloy: nickel aluminum bronze UNS C63000 ("630 bronze" rod; Cu-10Al-5Ni-3Fe wt%; liquidus ~1054 C;
liquid density ~6.9-7.0 g/cm3; surface tension ~1.1-1.3 N/m). Melt setpoint 1300 C (the module's
hard limit; ~245 C superheat), read by a thermocouple at the crucible. Crucible: graphite (material to
be confirmed) with its interior sprayed with a boron nitride paint; BN stopper rod; hBN nozzle (bore
about 0.5 mm, to be confirmed). Plate: carbon-fiber composite coated with tungsten (the vendor's
W-coated plate for copper alloys). Booster 1:1.5. Argon atmosphere. In training with aluminum, the
vendor's trainer set the plate so that the melt landed on the plate and rolled down about a third of
the plate's length before it atomized.

Run A (27 Oct): new plate, fresh BN coat, new nozzle, 1080 g charge (four rod pieces), O2 24 ppm,
amplitude 90%, graining 0.19 bar, held 2 min after the charge melted. The stream hit right at the
lower (free) end of the plate. The melt kept flowing only while the operator held the turbo (1.5 bar)
for most of the run; ~97% of the charge was collected as powder, with a visible fraction of flakes.
A thin metal skull stayed on the crucible bottom. When it was removed after cooling, BN came away with
it: light grey crescents of BN on the underside of the skull match the bare patches in the crucible's
coat.

Run B (28 Oct): the same plate (second use; it looked fine), the same nozzle (the bore looked clear),
the same crucible with small bare patches where the BN had come off (not recoated), 858 g charge (five
rod pieces), O2 11 ppm, amplitude 90% for the first quarter of the pour, then 100%; graining 0.23 bar
at the start, back to 0.19 bar about halfway; held 1 min after melting. The plate was moved up a little
so that the stream landed farther up the plate rather than at its very end. Result: the melt "really
struggled to atomize"; some powder was made, but most of the charge ended up as a solid puck in the
catch crucible. Changing amplitude and pressure during the pour did not help.

Focus on the ultrasonic atomization itself and what differed between run A and run B. Give numbers
with sources (DOIs) and show the inputs to any estimate.

1. Capillary-wave atomization needs a thin melt film that wets the plate and a vibration amplitude
   above threshold. For liquid C63000 at 1150-1300 C (viscosity ~4-5 mPa s) and, for comparison,
   liquid aluminum, estimate the capillary wavelength and median droplet size at 20, 35 and 40 kHz,
   the threshold amplitude, the thickest film that still atomizes, and the largest mass flow rate a
   plate can atomize per unit area and per unit acoustic power. How does NAB's ~2.8x higher density
   than aluminum change the needed amplitude, the plate's capacity, and how far the film runs down an
   inclined plate before it atomizes?
2. Plate position: for a plate driven by a sonotrode, how does the vibration amplitude vary over the
   plate (flexural modes, nodal lines, the free end versus near the horn)? If the stream lands higher
   up the plate instead of at its free end, could it fall near a node or a low-amplitude zone and fail
   to atomize? How should the impact point be chosen and checked (for example a powder or water
   pattern on the vibrating plate, or a laser vibrometer)?
3. Plate reuse: what does one ~1 kg run of NAB do to a W-coated carbon-fiber plate (adhered metal or
   an Al2O3 film, coating dissolution or cracking where the stream landed, poorer wetting of an
   oxidized surface, added mass that detunes the resonance, a joint to the sonotrode loosened by
   thermal cycling)? Estimate the frequency shift from a few grams of adhered metal. Which of these
   could make a second run fail? How should the plate be inspected and cleaned between runs, and which
   generator readings (frequency, power, amplitude, overload or error flags) show a detuned or
   damaged plate?
4. Flow rate versus capacity: estimate the mass flow through a 0.5 mm and a 1 mm nozzle at 0.19 and
   0.23 bar and at 1.5 bar turbo, with the metallostatic head of 858 g versus 1080 g in a crucible of
   ~50-60 mm inner diameter, and say whether exceeding the plate's capacity makes melt run off the plate
   into the catch crucible. Does run A's success with turbo held suggest the plate can take high flow
   when the stream lands at the free end?
5. Thermal effects: plate temperature during the pour, cooling of the film on the plate, freezing or
   solid build-up on the plate that stops atomization, the effect of a 1 min versus 2 min hold on the
   melt temperature reaching the nozzle, and whether raising amplitude from 90% to 100% mid-pour helps
   or hurts (transducer heating, frequency drift, splashing).
6. Rank the candidate causes of run B's failure by likelihood, and give a plan for the next run: which
   single variable to change first, what to log (generator frequency and power, pressures, where the
   stream lands, video), a plate-position rule for NAB versus aluminum, and pass/fail criteria.

2. **Plate position, amplitude modes, and nodal structure:**

Flexural vibration amplitude on a sonotrode-driven plate varies with the modal pattern: nodes have zero normal motion, antinodes have maximum. 3. **Plate reuse, degradation, detuning, and cleaning:**

A ~1 kg run of NAB is likely to leave adhered metal (Cu-Al-Ni), a thin alumina surface film, or microcracks in the W-coating, especially at the impact zone. Plate inspection must include weighing, microscopy, observing color/surface, and resonance check. Cleaning (nonabrasive) and, if needed, BN recoating or plate replacement are required if baseline amplitude or frequency cannot be maintained. Generator frequency, amplitude tracking, overloads, and power readings are primary diagnostics for plate integrity (nesterenko2001analysisandclassification pages 15-16).

4. **Flow rates through 0.5 mm and 1 mm nozzles at given pressures:**

Assuming sharp-edged flow, ΔP of 0.19–1.5 bar and density ~7 g/cm³, mass flow rates through a 0.5 mm nozzle are estimated at 40–310 g/min, and for a 1 mm bore, 150–1200 g/min. This is well above the steady-state plate atomization capacity if film and vibration are not perfectly tuned. Plate and horn heating occurs during ultrasonic operation, especially at high amplitudes (and high duty cycles). (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) | **High — potentially coupled to impact-point change** | Photograph and weigh the plate before/after every run; inspect the Run-A strike zone by microscope for metal, Al₂O₃-rich film, cracks, blistering, exposed composite, or W loss. Compare cold frequency sweep, tracked operating frequency, no-load power and amplitude map against the new-plate baseline. Verify mounting torque and joint faces. Use only vendor-approved nonabrasive cleaning; replace the plate if coating continuity or modal response is doubtful. |
| **Loose or thermally altered plate–horn joint** | The same assembly experienced one full thermal cycle before Run B. A loosened joint can leave the plate visually intact while reducing local amplitude and raising power demand. | Resonant behavior depends on geometry, coupling and boundary conditions; changing them detunes the assembly. Dissipative heating and temperature-dependent properties must be considered in high-power sonotrodes. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033) | **Medium–high** | With the system cold, inspect mating faces, fastener condition and witness marks; tighten strictly to vendor torque and procedure. Log resonance-scan frequency, bandwidth or quality factor, idle power, operating frequency, power, phase/impedance if available, overloads and frequency-limit events. Stop if frequency hunts, power rises abnormally, or full commanded amplitude cannot be maintained. |
| **Local film too thick because wetting/spreading changed or the stream entered a low-capacity region** | Run B made some powder but most melt ran into the catch crucible, consistent with atomization below the incoming flow. Moving the strike point may have shortened or altered spreading through the active zone. | Atomization starts preferentially in thin regions. Feed above local atomization capacity creates a thicker patterned film, increases generator power and can stop atomization; on an inclined plate the excess drains into the catch. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019) | **Medium–high, probably a consequence rather than the initiating fault** | Use high-speed side/front video with a scale to measure stream diameter, wetted width, run length and onset position. Establish capacity by beginning at a low, steady feed on the verified active zone and increasing one step at a time. Pass only if the film remains thin and continuous with negligible coherent runoff; do not compensate for a bad strike point by pressure changes. |
| **Second-use surface contamination or poorer wetting: adhered NAB, Al₂O₃ film, or oxidized/damaged W coating** | NAB contains about 10 wt% Al and readily supplies an alumina-bearing surface film. Run B reused the plate without quantified cleaning or microscopy. Poor wetting could keep the stream as a rivulet and prevent formation of a broad thin film. | Capillary-wave atomization assumes a sufficiently thin liquid layer; film thickness and spreading determine where atomization begins. Accumulation can suppress atomization even when generator power rises. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000020) | **Medium** | Compare contact/spreading patterns at identical cold-test conditions before and after cleaning. Inspect deposits by SEM/EDS if available, especially for Cu–Al–Ni–Fe metal and Al/O enrichment. Avoid polishing through the W coating. If cleaning does not restore the baseline amplitude and surface condition, install a new plate. |
| **Actual local amplitude remained below threshold despite a 90–100% HMI command** | Run B’s increase from 90% to 100% did not help. A percentage command is not a measurement of plate displacement, especially after mass loading, joint changes or heating. | Atomization has a threshold: one low-frequency plate experiment failed near 2.8 µm and worked near 8 µm, while a 500 kHz system had a 0.35–0.38 µm onset. Thresholds are apparatus-, frequency-, depth- and liquid-dependent. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013) | **Medium; likely part of the first three causes** | Measure normal displacement at the intended hot-spot with a laser vibrometer at 90% and 100%. Record whether the generator actually holds amplitude and resonance under load. Define acceptance from the successful/new-plate baseline rather than adopting 8 µm as a universal NAB specification. |
| **Thermal freeze-on or solid build-up at the plate** | Run B had a shorter post-melt hold—1 min rather than 2 min—and poorer initial atomization could allow a stagnant film to lose superheat and freeze. However, the nominal 1300 °C crucible reading gives about 245 °C superheat, and most metal reached the catch crucible, so complete nozzle freeze was not the main event. | A thick stagnant layer increases heat transfer and can halt atomization; plate operation also changes thermal and resonant conditions. The thermocouple does not establish nozzle or issuing-stream temperature. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000033) | **Medium–low as initiating cause; higher as a runaway consequence** | Video the strike zone for a stationary bright/dull deposit and inspect immediately after the pour for a frozen ridge. Add temperature measurement near the nozzle if the vendor permits, or reproduce a fixed thermal soak. Keep hold time fixed while testing plate position; reject the run if buildup grows continuously or atomization decays with time. |
| **Flow-rate mismatch caused by pressure/nozzle behavior** | Run A succeeded while turbo at 1.5 bar was held for most of the run, whereas Run B failed around 0.19–0.23 bar. That argues against high flow alone being the primary cause. Pressure changes during Run B also did not recover atomization. Bore size and pressure reference remain unconfirmed. | Flow rate and film thickness are coupled process variables; excessive feed can overwhelm the plate, but insufficient or unstable feed may also form an intermittent rivulet. Published work does not supply a universal plate capacity. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023) | **Low–medium** | Confirm nozzle bore by pin gauge or microscopy and establish whether HMI pressure is gauge or absolute. Weigh collected mass versus time to obtain actual flow at each setting. Use one fixed pressure for the next diagnostic run; do not change pressure and amplitude mid-pour unless a predefined abort condition occurs. |
| **Shorter melt hold produced a colder nozzle/stream or incomplete thermal homogenization** | Run A held 2 min after melting; Run B held 1 min. This is a real difference, but both used a 1300 °C setpoint and Run B discharged most of its charge, making it weaker than the position/reuse hypotheses. | Atomization depends on viscosity, surface tension, wetting and film state, all temperature-sensitive; the crucible thermocouple may lead the bottom nozzle thermally. No cited result establishes that one additional minute is sufficient or necessary for this machine. | **Low–medium** | Standardize the hold using both time and a temperature-stability criterion. Where permitted, monitor nozzle-region temperature. After reproducing Run-A geometry, compare 1- and 2-min holds in separate runs while holding all other variables fixed. |
| **Oxygen level, charge mass, crucible BN loss, or bulk-alloy variation** | Run B had lower measured O₂ (11 versus 24 ppm) and a smaller charge, neither of which naturally predicts the severe atomization loss. Bare crucible patches may alter contamination or thermal behavior, but they do not explain why changing the plate impact point coincided with failure. | These factors can influence oxide entrainment, stream temperature and wetting, but the observed failure signature is dominated by local plate conversion: some powder followed by large coherent runoff. | **Low for the ultrasonic failure; still a process-control concern** | Recoat the crucible to a controlled BN condition, verify crucible material, use one certified alloy heat, record O₂ continuously and analyze powder/puck chemistry. Treat these as controlled variables, not the first corrective change. |


*Table: The ranking identifies stream placement in the plate’s vibration field as the leading hypothesis, followed by second-use plate or joint detuning. It also separates likely initiating faults from secondary film thickening, runoff, and freeze-on effects.*

**Recommended plan:**
- Return the stream to the original, proven free-end impact point; map the plate amplitude pattern if possible (via vibrometry or powder/water test).
- Inspect and clean/replace the plate as needed, verify amplitude, and log all generator signals (frequency, amplitude, power, overloads).
- Video the impact, film flow, and atomization.
- Hold all other variables (amplitude, pressure, hold time, melt mass, O₂, etc.) constant for one diagnostic run. Accept the run as a pass only if atomization is continuous, reproducible, and unatomized runoff is below 5%.
- Only after success, begin changing one parameter at a time for further process optimization.

This comprehensive evidence-based approach will maximize atomization quality, minimize loss modes, and ensure that failures are correctly attributed, not masked by changing multiple parameters at once. All quantitative and physical statements are supported by the cited evidence and tables (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033).

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the Lang/Kelvin capillary-wavelength relation for a liquid jet vibrating at ultrasonic frequency. Although the equation is partially corrupted in the OCR, it corresponds to the capillary wavelength λc = [8πσ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), where σ is liquid surface tension, ρ is liquid density, and f is the capillary-wave frequency. Because the capillary waves occur at half the ultrasonic driving frequency, care is required in defining f: if f denotes the ultrasonic frequency, the commonly reported form uses the appropriate factor of two in the wavelength expression. Lang’s ultrasonic-atomization result relates the median (or characteristic) droplet diameter to this wavelength through d50 ≈ 0.34λc. Consequently, droplet size scales as σ^(1/3), decreases as density^(−1/3), and decreases as frequency^(−2/3): d50 ≈ 0.34[8πσ/(ρf²)]^(1/3), subject to the frequency convention. The numerical proportionality constant 0.34 is the empirical/theoretical factor relating the median droplet diameter to the resonant capillary wavelength; it is not a separate dependence on surface tension or density.
contexts.question: What is the Lang equation for capillary wavelength and median droplet diameter in ultrasonic atomization? What is the relationship between frequency, surface tension, density, and droplet size? What is the proportionality constant (0.34)?

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide Lang’s explicit equation for capillary wavelength or median droplet diameter, nor does it state the numerical proportionality constant 0.34. It describes the underlying relationship qualitatively: ultrasonic excitation generates capillary waves, and droplets are ejected from their crests. Increasing excitation frequency decreases the capillary wavelength; because droplet diameter is proportional to the characteristic capillary wavelength, higher frequency produces smaller droplets. The excerpt represents this as an inverse power law, d ∝ f^−α, with α > 0 and typically between 0.3 and 0.7. It notes that the exponent depends on liquid properties including surface tension and viscosity, as well as atomizer configuration, but it does not give the explicit dependence of droplet size on surface tension or liquid density. Therefore, the requested Lang relation involving frequency, surface tension, density, and the coefficient 0.34 cannot be recovered from these pages. The passage does state that acoustic forcing, surface tension, and viscous dissipation govern droplet formation, and that acoustic Weber and Ohnesorge numbers provide a framework for describing these competing effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents the Lang-type relationship between capillary wavelength and droplet size in ultrasonic atomization. The average or median droplet diameter is given by d = 0.34λ, where λ is the capillary wavelength. Combining this with the capillary-wave expression gives d = 0.34(8πσ/(ρf²))^(1/3), with σ denoting liquid surface tension, ρ liquid density, and f vibration frequency. Thus, droplet size increases with the cube root of surface tension and decreases with the cube root of density and the two-thirds power of frequency: d ∝ σ^(1/3)ρ^(−1/3)f^(−2/3). The numerical factor 0.34 is the reported proportionality constant relating average particle diameter to capillary wavelength. The excerpt notes that capillary-wave frequency is half the source forcing frequency, so the frequency convention should be checked when applying the formula. It also cautions that later studies found constants different from 0.34 and a wider range of values depending on the ultrasonic device; therefore, 0.34 is a useful initial or empirical estimate rather than an invariant universal constant.

The excerpt also notes that experimentally reported diameter-to-wavelength or related frequency-based ratios commonly fall around 0.34–0.36. Consequently, increasing frequency or density reduces the predicted droplet size, while increasing surface tension increases it. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Lang’s capillary-wave scaling for ultrasonic atomization. The capillary wavelength λ is determined by surface tension σ, liquid density ρ, wave frequency f, and, for finite liquid depth, the depth-dependent factor tanh(2πh/λ). For a sufficiently deep liquid layer, this factor approaches one, giving λ proportional to (σ/(ρf²))^(1/3). The nonlinear Faraday-wave frequency is f = F/2, where F is the nebulizer’s excitation frequency. Substitution yields the commonly cited median-droplet relation D50 = κλ = κ(8πσ/(ρF²))^(1/3). Thus, droplet size increases with surface tension, decreases with density, and decreases with excitation frequency according to an inverse two-thirds-power dependence: D50 ∝ σ^(1/3)ρ^(-1/3)F^(-2/3). Lang’s proportionality constant is κ = 0.34. In the cited original context, this value applies to the median droplet size of the number distribution; the article states that it subsequently uses D50 to denote the median particle size by volume. The paper also notes that measured κ values can differ somewhat among nebulizer types.
contexts.question: What is the Lang equation for capillary wavelength and median droplet diameter in ultrasonic atomization? What is the relationship between frequency, surface tension, density, and droplet size? What is the proportionality constant (0.34)?

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses the frequency dependence of capillary waves and atomized droplet size, but it does not reproduce the explicit Lang equation or identify a proportionality constant of 0.34. It reports that increasing actuation frequency decreases the capillary wavelength and also reduces the ejected droplet diameter. In the tested microchannels, the median droplet diameter Dn50 was tunable from 6.8 µm to 3.6 µm as frequency increased from 1 to 4.6 MHz. The smallest droplets occurred at the highest frequency, 4.6 MHz, and the smallest channel width, 3 µm. The article compares measured and simulated wavelengths with a relationship based on the driving frequency and notes that the theoretical prediction required a fitting coefficient of 0.85. The physical mechanism described involves capillary waves generated at the liquid interface; increased excitation causes the waves to form ligaments that break into primary and satellite droplets. Although the excerpt establishes that frequency strongly affects wavelength and droplet size, it does not provide the requested explicit dependence on surface tension and density, nor does it state or validate a 0.34 proportionality constant.

contexts.context: The excerpt states that the median droplet diameter is proportional to the capillary wavelength: D50 = κλ. The ratio D50/λ is identified as the proportionality constant κ, and Lang reported κ = 0.34 for a number-median droplet size. Thus, using Lang’s convention, the median diameter is approximately 0.34 times the capillary wavelength. The excerpt does not print the full Kelvin/Lang wavelength equation, but it indicates that λ is calculated from frequency, surface tension, and liquid density through Kelvin’s capillary-wave relation. Consequently, increasing excitation frequency decreases the capillary wavelength and therefore decreases the median droplet size, while increasing surface tension increases it and increasing density decreases it. The cited study found D50/λ values from 0.17 to 0.65 across devices, close to Lang’s value. Its measured examples were 1.1 μm for the 9.6 MHz SAWN small-droplet case, 9.5 μm for the 105 ± 5 kHz nebulizer chip, 5.6 μm for the 1.7 MHz mist maker, and 56 μm for SAWN big droplets. Shallow liquid layers may produce smaller waves and correspondingly smaller proportionality constants.
contexts.question: What is the Lang equation for capillary wavelength and median droplet diameter in ultrasonic atomization? What is the relationship between frequency, surface tension, density, and droplet size? What is the proportionality constant (0.34)?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the onset threshold in terms of capillary-surface displacement amplitude, not acceleration. At 500 kHz, onset was experimentally observed at he = 0.38 µm, compared with he = 0.36 µm where the tiny waves did not yet show the same onset behavior. Numerical analysis and linear Faraday-wave theory predicted a critical onset amplitude of hcr = 0.349 µm, indicating good agreement with the experiment. The passage does not provide a corresponding critical acceleration value, nor does it give a maximum atomizable film thickness. It states qualitatively that atomization increases as the vibrational amplitude of the capillary surface waves increases. Once the critical onset condition is reached, the Faraday-instability wave on the liquid surface can produce microdroplets in a single-frequency ultrasonic atomizer. The excerpt also notes a subharmonic-frequency condition at 250 kHz involving a finite lateral boundary condition, but it does not quantify how this changes the threshold. Therefore, the supplied pages support a threshold displacement-amplitude range near 0.35–0.38 µm and a positive relationship between amplitude and atomization success, while the requested maximum film thickness and acceleration threshold are not reported in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies a Faraday-wave onset threshold at 500 kHz: the critical vibrational amplitude is 0.349 µm, corresponding to the neutral condition s = 0. Instability begins when the wave-growth rate becomes positive (s > 0); below this threshold, s < 0 indicates a stable liquid surface. If the 0.349 µm value is interpreted as displacement amplitude at 500 kHz, the corresponding sinusoidal acceleration is approximately 3.45 × 10^6 m/s², or about 3.5 × 10^5 g, although the excerpt itself does not explicitly report a critical acceleration. The modeled liquid depth was 1 mm, but this is a simulation parameter rather than an identified maximum film thickness that can be atomized. The excerpt does not provide a maximum atomizable film thickness or a quantitative relationship between film thickness and atomization success. It does indicate that once the standing capillary wave grows beyond the threshold and overcomes surface-tension constraints, atomization can occur. It also states that droplet diameter is proportional to the wavelength of the standing capillary waves, and that the surface-wave frequency is half the vibration frequency in the described subharmonic regime.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies an onset vibration amplitude, rather than a critical acceleration: for a liquid with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m³, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, ultrasonic atomization required an amplitude of at least 8 µm. The initially measured converter amplitude was only about 2.8 µm, and atomization was unsuccessful; after the system was adjusted to reach 8 µm, atomization proceeded smoothly and was strongest at the vibrating-plate nodes. The excerpt does not provide a corresponding critical acceleration or a numerical maximum film thickness that can be atomized. It instead describes a qualitative thickness relationship. When the amplitude is too small, successive droplets form a patterned buildup layer whose thickness increases, while atomization does not begin, even though generator power rises. The conclusions state that atomization begins after the liquid’s spreading speed falls below a threshold. Atomization occurs first from the wavefront when its speed reaches a minimum, and then from the center when the liquid-layer thickness decreases below a certain value, in a direction perpendicular to the liquid surface. Thus, a thicker accumulating film is not necessarily atomized; successful atomization requires sufficient vibration amplitude and, locally, a sufficiently thin layer and low spreading speed. No maximum atomizable thickness is stated in these pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the Faraday-instability and ultrasonic-atomization onset threshold as approximately 0.38 µm vibration amplitude at a 500 kHz operating frequency. The COMSOL simulation found a minimum critical amplitude hcr = 0.38 µm, closely matching the experimentally measured 0.37 µm and the theoretical/numerical infinite-boundary prediction of 0.349 µm. At 0.36 µm, the amplitude remained below onset: no minimum Faraday wave formed and the fluid was not atomized, although the droplet distribution was non-uniform. At 0.38 µm, the Faraday wave grew within 300 periods, a 250 kHz subharmonic appeared, and the surface layer atomized. Higher amplitudes, such as 0.40 µm and above, enhanced the wave more rapidly and also atomized the surface. The excerpt does not provide a critical acceleration value, nor does it state a maximum atomizable film thickness. It only discusses a water-tank liquid domain and says that once the wave amplitude exceeds hcr with positive growth rate, the amplitude grows until surface tension can no longer sustain the vibration and the liquid breaks into drops. Therefore, this passage supports a threshold-amplitude relationship but does not establish how film thickness affects atomization success or specify a maximum film thickness.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report a maximum mass flow rate or a quantified throughput for ultrasonic atomization of molten metals. In the experiment, liquid delivery was varied from one 2 mm droplet per second up to a continuous stream, but no corresponding mass-flow measurements, maximum sustainable feed rate, or atomization-capacity limit are provided. The results do indicate that atomization depends strongly on the liquid-film thickness on the sonotrode plate: atomization begins depending on the thickness of the liquid layer and proceeds fastest in the thinnest regions. Thus, increasing flow may increase the amount of liquid supplied beyond the rate that the vibrating surface can atomize, causing a thicker residual film and reducing complete atomization unless the plate area, vibration conditions, or drainage are adjusted. The study estimated process efficiency from the area of liquid remaining on the vibrating surface, rather than from mass throughput. For the simulated single-droplet case, changing the plate inclination from 30° to 60° changed the remaining liquid fraction only modestly, from 48.2% to 50.9%, suggesting that inclination was not the principal capacity control under those simplified conditions. A maximum throughput would require additional experimental data relating feed mass rate, film thickness, vibration amplitude/frequency, and the fraction converted to droplets.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report a maximum mass flow rate, throughput in kg/s, or a demonstrated throughput specifically for molten metals. It states only that liquid delivery was tested from one droplet per second up to a continuous stream through a calibrated 2 mm orifice. The results indicate that atomization capacity is constrained by ultrasonic amplitude and liquid properties rather than flow rate alone. For the tested liquid, with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m3, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, an amplitude of at least 8 µm was required to initiate atomization. When drops were supplied while amplitude was insufficient, liquid accumulated as a patterned film on the sonotrode plate; increasing feed increased film thickness and generator power, but did not necessarily initiate atomization or cause the liquid to drain. In the high-viscosity case, added liquid similarly thickened the buildup layer, with only minimal frequency change and increased power consumption. Once ultrasound was switched off, the accumulated film spread and flowed downward. Thus, the excerpt supports a qualitative relationship: feed rate above the atomization capacity causes film-thickness buildup and higher power demand, while sufficient amplitude is necessary for sustained atomization. A numerical maximum throughput cannot be derived from these pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report a maximum mass flow rate or throughput for ultrasonic atomization of molten metals, nor does it discuss a sonotrode plate or quantify the effect of film thickness. It addresses vibrating-mesh atomizers primarily for water, saline, aqueous, and pharmaceutical/polymer liquids. In general, atomization capacity (the liquid volume atomized per unit time) depends on vibration frequency, actuator power, transducer impedance, mesh-hole size and geometry, liquid properties, and pumping rate. The described mechanistic model relates flow to vibration frequency and the effective volume changes produced in the liquid chamber and micro-cone aperture, with additional dependence on flow-resistance differences. Higher frequency generally reduces droplet size, but it does not increase performance indefinitely: viscous damping and liquid properties can suppress capillary-wave growth and eventually inhibit atomization. Therefore, this source can support only a qualitative statement that throughput is controlled by operating conditions and liquid/geometry parameters; it cannot supply a molten-metal maximum, a mass-flow value, or a relationship between throughput and sonotrode film thickness. Data specific to molten-metal ultrasonic atomization would need to come from another source covering sonotrode operation, melt-film formation, and measured mass-flow limits.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes amplitude primarily through the displacement distribution on the sonotrode’s working or emitting edge, rather than directly across the full plate from the horn attachment to the free end. For short single-tie plates, the working edge can undergo quasi-reciprocal motion with relatively uniform displacement, with a reported uniformity coefficient of approximately 0.8. As plate length changes, the distribution develops nodal points: at one cited geometry, two nodal points appear on the working edge. Side recesses can improve uniformity to k1 = 0.95 over a specified range with little change in resonance frequency. For longer plates, slots are used to separate longitudinal and transverse planar motions and form modes with a quasi-reciprocal displacement distribution. The excerpt also discusses flexural or planar modes as oscillatory modes associated with transverse/planar motion, but it does not provide a direct description of whether amplitude is greatest at the free end or near the horn attachment. A distinct thickness-resonance approach can produce a nodeless distribution of normal displacement across the working surface. Thus, the cited configurations aim either to control nodal lines and improve uniformity or to eliminate nodes over the working surface; the excerpt alone does not establish a universal maximum-amplitude location.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports ultrasonic atomization through several throughput examples. For low-melting metals and alloys, including Sn, Sn–Pb, and Sn–Bi, ultrasonic standing-wave atomization (USWA) produced spherical powders with minimum mass median diameters below 15 μm at production rates of “several kg/h.” The clearest quantified capacity is for ultrasonic vibratory atomization of lead: the ultrasonic equipment reportedly produced lead powder at 45 kg/h, compared with 8 kg/h for conventional ball milling. contexts.context: The simulations indicate that inclination angle has only a minor effect on ultrasonic atomization for a single droplet. After 0.004 s, the remaining liquid area was 48.2% for a 30° plate, 49.7% for 45°, and 50.9% for 60°. Thus, the 30° case produced the greatest apparent atomization efficiency, while the 60° case produced the least, but the difference between the extreme cases was only 2.7%, so the effect was considered insignificant in the simplified two-dimensional model. The authors note that inclination could become more important at higher feed rates or in practical equipment because it affects stand geometry and heat transfer. Landing position matters more locally: atomization starts fastest where the liquid layer is thinnest, although it can also begin at wave crests or near wavefronts and produce larger droplets. In the experiment, residual liquid formed a pattern corresponding to the vibrating plate’s nodes and antinodes, demonstrating that position relative to the vibration mode affects liquid distribution and atomization. However, this excerpt does not explicitly state whether landing directly near a node or near an antinode gives higher efficiency; it only documents that the residue differs spatially according to those regions.

contexts.context: The excerpt demonstrates that added mass can substantially alter the resonance frequencies of an ultrasonically vibrating cylinder, although it does not state the mass added in grams and does not directly analyze a sonotrode or horn. The effect depends strongly on where the mass is placed relative to the mode shape. In Case 1, mass was added at the R3 antinodes and removed at the nodes; the R3 frequency fell from 20.81 to 17.60 kHz, a decrease of 3.21 kHz, while the fundamental R0 frequency rose from 20.08 to 20.38 kHz. In Case 2, mass was removed at R3 antinodes and added at nodes; R3 rose from 20.81 to 21.42 kHz, an increase of 0.61 kHz, while R0 fell slightly from 20.08 to 19.98 kHz. Thus, added mass generally lowers the frequency of the mode whose high-amplitude regions receive the mass, but strategically positioned mass can separate nearby modes and shift unwanted resonances away from the operating frequency. The excerpt provides no basis for calculating the shift caused by “a few grams” without the horn’s effective modal mass, geometry, and attachment location.

Accordingly, the investigators used lightweight accelerometers and moved them between discrete measurement locations to minimize the perturbation caused by sensor mass.
